lessons.explanation:
Every Go variable starts at its type's zero value: `0` for numbers, `""` for strings, `false` for booleans, and `nil` for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions and interfaces. A declaration gives you a defined value immediately.

A struct starts with every field at its own zero value. Design that state to be useful when possible: counters and slices work naturally, while a map field still needs initialization before a write. A `New` function is useful when the type requires setup that its zero value cannot provide.
lessons.objective: Predict the value of any declared variable before it is assigned.
lessons.question: What does this print, and why does len work on a nil slice?
lessons.title: Nothing is uninitialised

lessons.explanation:
`:=` declares and assigns in one step inside a function. At least one non-blank name on the left must be new in the current block; otherwise the compiler reports "no new variables".

A short declaration may mix new names with names already declared in that same block. Inside a nested block, however, it may introduce a different variable with the same spelling. Use `=` when the intention is to update an existing variable.
lessons.objective: Choose between := and = without guessing, and know when := is illegal.
lessons.title: := declares, = assigns

lessons.explanation: A useful way to read Go is to ask three questions at each assignment: which block owns this name, what type does it have, and is a new variable being created? The spelling of a name alone does not answer any of them.
lessons.objective: Follow values through a short declaration, an assignment and a shadowed name without running the program.

sections.body: Start with a local variable. Its type comes from the expression on the right. An ordinary assignment updates that same variable; it does not create another binding. Read the two lines as a small state table: first count is 2, then count is 5.
sections.code:
count := 2
count = count + 3
fmt.Println(count) // 5
sections.title: Trace the original variable
sections.walkthrough: The right side is evaluated before the assignment. The old count contributes 2, the expression becomes 5, and only then is count updated. This is useful when stepping through a counter, an index or a retry budget.

sections.body: An if body is a new lexical block. A short declaration there may hide an outer variable. This can be intentional for a temporary result, but it becomes confusing when the outer result was supposed to change.
sections.title: A nested block owns a different name
sections.walkthrough: The inner name stops being accessible at the closing brace. Replacing its := with = would instead update the outer string. The difference is scope, not a special rule about if.

sections.body: In a multi-name short declaration, at least one non-blank name must be new in the same block. Existing names in that block keep their declared types. Before changing := to =, find every declaration and branch exit; an inner err may be a deliberate short-lived error, or it may hide the value returned later.
sections.title: Use the rule while reviewing real code

reading.takeaway: Read the block before the operator. Prefer a short temporary scope when it clarifies ownership; use assignment when an existing result must change.

lessons.title: Read a declaration one scope at a time

lessons.explanation: An error result is part of a function contract. The caller needs to know whether a value is valid when err is non-nil, who should add context, and which layer decides what the user sees. A short early return makes that contract visible.
lessons.objective: Trace a result and error through a complete boundary, including wrapping and partial results.

sections.body: This function promises a useful positive integer only when its error is nil. Invalid syntax and a non-positive number are different failures. In each failure branch, return immediately; the normal result appears once at the bottom.
sections.title: Trace both returns
sections.walkthrough: For "abc", Atoi fails and the first branch exits. For "0", parsing succeeds and validation fails. For "8", neither error branch runs and the caller receives 8, nil. No exception handler is needed to follow those paths.

sections.body: The helper adds operation context without choosing an HTTP status or printing to a console. A CLI handler or HTTP adapter can decide how to report the error. Avoid logging the same error at every layer; repeated messages obscure a single failure.
sections.title: Handle it at the boundary

sections.body: Some APIs deliberately return useful data with an error. io.Reader is a notable example: process the bytes returned before deciding what the error means. Do not generalize the early-return pattern into discarding all non-zero results. Read the particular API contract and distinguish expected absence, invalid input and infrastructure failure.
sections.title: Partial results need a documented contract

reading.takeaway: Follow each return as a pair. Handle errors deliberately, preserve a useful cause with wrapping, and use partial values only when the API promises them.

lessons.title: Read the failure path before the happy path

lessons.explanation:
Go functions can return several values. A common fallible signature returns a result followed by `error`; callers inspect that error before continuing with the result.

This makes ordinary failures explicit at the call site instead of using exceptions. Go also has `panic` and `recover` for exceptional control flow, but an error result is the usual contract for an expected failure. Short failure branches keep the successful path easy to read.
lessons.objective: Write a function that returns a result and an error, and read one.
lessons.title: Two returns instead of one exception

lessons.explanation:
Go refuses to compile a function with a variable it never reads, and a file with an import it never uses. Not a warning — an error.

This feels hostile for about a week. What it buys is that dead code cannot accumulate quietly, and that a half-finished edit fails loudly instead of shipping. The escape hatch when you genuinely need it is assignment to _, which says "deliberately discarded" out loud.
lessons.objective: Recognise the two unused errors on sight and know why they exist.
lessons.title: An unused variable stops the build

lessons.explanation:
An untyped constant in Go has arbitrary precision and no type until it is used. `const big = 1 << 62` is fine even where an int is 32 bits, because nothing has asked it to become an int yet. The moment it is assigned or passed, it takes the type it is needed as — and that is where it can fail to fit.

`iota` is the other half. Inside a const block it counts from zero, one step per line, which is how Go writes enumerations without an enum keyword. The idiom is worth recognising on sight: a type, a const block with iota, and often a String method.
lessons.objective: Explain why 1 << 40 compiles as a constant but overflows as an int32.
lessons.question: What does this print?
lessons.source:
package main

import "fmt"

type Level int

const (
	Debug Level = iota
	Info
	Warn
	Error
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println(Debug, Info, Warn, Error)
	const big = 1 << 40
	fmt.Println(big / 1024 / 1024 / 1024)
}
lessons.title: Constants have no type until they need one

lessons.explanation:
In C, Java and JavaScript a case runs on into the next one unless you write `break`. Go inverted that: a case ends at the next case, and `fallthrough` is the keyword you write on the rare occasion you want the old behaviour. You do not need `break` just to end a case, though an explicit `break` can leave a switch early.

Two more differences worth having: a case can list several values separated by commas, and a switch with no expression is a tidy way to write a chain of conditions.
lessons.objective: Write a Go switch without reaching for break.
lessons.title: switch does not fall through

lessons.explanation:
There is no implicit numeric conversion in Go. An int and an int64 are different types even where they are the same width, and adding them is an error rather than a promotion. The fix is always an explicit conversion, and the point of the rule is that the place where precision could be lost is visible in the source.

A named type behaves the same way. `type Celsius float64` cannot be added to a float64 without saying so, which is exactly what makes named types worth declaring: the compiler stops you mixing units.
lessons.objective: Fix a mismatched-type expression without guessing.
lessons.title: Go never converts a number for you

lessons.explanation:
Names in a function's result list declare local result variables initialized to zero. A bare `return` returns their current values. In a short helper, names such as `quot` and `rem` can explain which result is which.

An explicit `return quot, rem` is often easier to review once a function has branches. Result names document intent, but the compiler does not protect two same-typed results from being swapped. A deferred closure may change named results before the function returns to its caller.
lessons.objective: Write a short function that uses a naked return, and know when not to.
lessons.title: A return can name what it is handing back

lessons.explanation:
Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order when the surrounding function returns. Three `defer fmt.Println(n)` statements execute in the reverse of their registration order.

The deferred function and its arguments are evaluated when `defer` executes. A deferred closure, in contrast, may read a captured variable when it eventually runs. Keep that distinction clear when a variable changes between registration and return.
lessons.objective: Say the print order of three deferred calls.
lessons.question: What does this print? The Tour's stacking-defers program.
lessons.title: Deferred calls stack, last one first

summary: Declarations, zero values, multiple returns and the shapes Go repeats everywhere.
title: Go core
translationNote: Most of this unit is not new material — it is unlearning. Go has no built-in class constructors or exception-handling syntax, and declared variables start with zero values, so habits from Java, C# and Python each need one specific adjustment rather than a general rewrite.

lessons.explanation:
A struct groups fields under a type name. `Point{X: 1, Y: 2}` names its fields; `Point{1, 2}` relies on declaration order. Reordering same-typed fields can silently change an unkeyed literal's meaning. Adding a field usually makes an existing unkeyed literal fail to compile. Keyed literals make intent clearer, and vet checks unkeyed literals for structs from other packages.

A struct's zero value is a struct, not nil. Each field begins at its own zero value. Fields beginning with an uppercase letter are exported; visibility is decided per field.
lessons.objective: Declare a struct type and build values of it without positional guessing.
lessons.title: A struct is data, and its fields have names

lessons.explanation:
A method is declared outside the type, with the receiver in parentheses before the name: `func (r Rect) Area() int`. There is no class body, and methods can be attached to any type you declared in this package — including `type Celsius float64`, not only structs.

The receiver is a copy unless it is a pointer. `func (r Rect) Grow()` mutates a copy and the caller sees nothing; `func (r *Rect) Grow()` mutates the original. Go calls either form for you — `r.Grow()` works on an addressable value whichever receiver you chose — so the compiler will not warn you that the mutation went nowhere.

The convention is to pick one kind of receiver for the whole type. A type with some value methods and some pointer methods has a method set that changes depending on whether you hold a value or a pointer, and that is where "it does not satisfy the interface" comes from.
lessons.objective: Put a method on your own type and choose the receiver deliberately.
lessons.title: A method is a function with a receiver

lessons.explanation:
Go passes everything by value. A struct handed to a function is copied, and writing to the copy changes nothing the caller can see. A pointer is how you say "the same one", and `&` and `*` are the whole syntax: `&value` takes an address, `*pointer` reads through one. Field access needs no `*` — `p.X` works on a pointer as well as a value, which is why you rarely see the star in ordinary code.

There is no pointer arithmetic. A Go pointer either points at something or is nil, and that is all it can do — which is why passing one is safe in a way it is not in C.

The reason to use one is mutation. "Pointers are faster" is a guess: for a small struct the copy is often cheaper than the indirection and the extra work the garbage collector inherits. Measure before believing it, and until you have, choose based on whether the callee needs to change what it was given.
lessons.objective: Say when a pointer is required and when it is only noise.
lessons.question: What are the two numbers, and why are they different?
lessons.title: A pointer is for changing something, not for speed

lessons.explanation:
Functions are values: they can be stored, passed and returned. A function literal keeps access to the variables it captures, rather than taking an automatic snapshot of their values.

Two closures capturing the same variable see each other's updates. Separate calls to a factory create separate environments. When you need a snapshot, make an explicit copy for the closure to capture.

Since Go 1.22, iteration variables declared by a loop get a fresh variable on each iteration. A loop assigning to a variable declared outside it still reuses that variable. The distinction between `:=` and `=` matters here too.
lessons.objective: Return a function that carries state, and know what it captured.
lessons.title: A function is a value, and it remembers where it came from

lessons.explanation:
In C this is the classic mistake: return the address of a local and the stack frame is gone by the time the caller looks. Go removes the mistake rather than warning about it. The compiler works out that the value outlives the function — escape analysis — and allocates it somewhere that survives.

So `return &Config{}` is ordinary, idiomatic Go, and constructors called `New...` do it constantly. You are not choosing stack or heap; the compiler is, from how the value is used.

What this does *not* mean is that pointers are free. An escaping value becomes garbage collector work, which is the real cost behind "pointers are faster" being a guess rather than a rule.
lessons.objective: Explain why Go lets you return the address of a local variable.
lessons.question: Does this compile, and what does it print?
lessons.title: Returning a pointer to a local is fine

summary: Structs, methods, pointers, and functions that are values.
title: Types you define
translationNote:
There is no class here and nothing to inherit from. A struct is data, a method is a function with a receiver written before its name, and the two are declared separately — which means you can put methods on any type you define, not only on structs.

The habit to unlearn is reaching for a pointer by default. In Go a value is copied unless you say otherwise, and that is usually what you want; a pointer is for when the method has to change the thing it was called on, or when copying it would genuinely cost.

lessons.explanation: A slice describes a region of an array. Copying a slice value copies its descriptor, not all the elements. Two descriptors may therefore refer to the same elements while having different lengths and capacities.
lessons.objective: Predict a subslice, an element write and append by tracking the backing array.

sections.body: Treat the array as three numbered cells and each slice as a window over those cells. b begins at the second cell of a. Updating b[0] changes that cell; a observes it because it still refers to the same array.
sections.title: Draw the shared storage
sections.walkthrough: No goroutines are involved here. This is aliasing in a single execution flow. It matters for helper functions that appear to return a fresh view but actually let their callers change the original data.

sections.body: Append may reuse storage when capacity is available, or allocate storage when it is not. Assign its result because the returned descriptor can change. A full slice expression can restrict capacity, preventing an append through that view from using the hidden tail; existing element writes still share storage.
sections.title: Capacity affects append, not ownership
sections.walkthrough: This append must grow beyond b's capacity. Do not depend on a particular capacity growth factor; the language does not promise one.

sections.body: Use slices.Clone for an independent shallow copy of the elements. For slices of pointers or nested slices, the pointed-to objects remain shared. Decide whether you need a view, a shallow clone, or a domain-specific deep copy. Write that decision into the function contract instead of leaving callers to guess.
sections.title: Choose a copy at the ownership boundary

reading.takeaway: Track array identity as well as len and cap. A different slice value can still expose the same mutable storage.

lessons.title: A slice is a window, not a copied array

lessons.explanation:
A slice is three words: a pointer to an array, a length and a capacity. append writes into the existing array while the capacity allows it, and allocates a new one when it does not.

That single rule explains most slice surprises: whether a write is seen by another slice depends on whether an append happened to reallocate.
lessons.objective: Predict when append allocates and when it writes in place.
lessons.question: What are the two length and capacity pairs?
lessons.source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := make([]int, 0, 4)
	s = append(s, 1, 2)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
	s = append(s, 3, 4, 5)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
}
lessons.title: len is what you have, cap is what you can grow into

lessons.explanation:
Slicing does not copy elements. `s[1:3]` refers to the same backing array, so writes to overlapping elements are visible through both slices. An append that allocates a new array detaches the returned slice from that old storage.

A full slice expression such as `s[1:3:3]` limits capacity, forcing an append of another element to allocate. It does not detach the elements already in the view. Use `copy` or `slices.Clone` when the result must be independently mutable.
lessons.objective: Spot the moment a subslice starts sharing writes with its parent.
lessons.title: Two slices, one array

lessons.explanation: A goroutine does not make its arguments private. If two workers share a slice, you must reason about the slice descriptor and the array it refers to. Making extra goroutines can expose an ownership mistake that a sequential example concealed.
lessons.objective: Separate shared headers, shared elements and safe collection of concurrent results.

sections.body: Concurrent append to one shared slice variable reads and writes the same descriptor and may write the same backing storage. Even if capacity is large enough, append still changes the shared length. Reserving capacity is a performance choice, not synchronization.
sections.code:
// Unsafe: both goroutines update the same slice.
var results []int
go func() { results = append(results, 1) }()
go func() { results = append(results, 2) }()
sections.title: Why append needs coordination
sections.walkthrough: The outcome is not a reliable permutation of [1 2]. This is a deliberate counterexample, not code to copy. A passing test without the race detector does not establish safety.

sections.body: A pre-sized slice permits independent element writes when each worker owns a different index, no worker changes the descriptor, and the reader waits for every writer. Elements that themselves contain shared pointers need their own ownership rules.
sections.title: Give each worker a separate slot
sections.walkthrough: Index i is assigned to exactly one goroutine. WaitGroup orders the final read after the completed writes. For very large inputs, combine this ownership pattern with a bounded worker pool rather than starting a goroutine per item.

sections.body: If each job returns an unknown number of values, let workers send results to one owner that appends, or protect every access with the same mutex. A channel transfers values; it does not deep-copy a slice payload. The sender must stop mutating transferred storage or clone it first. Run race-enabled tests on a supported desktop toolchain; the app does not offer a native race detector.
sections.title: Use a single collector for variable-length output

reading.takeaway: Concurrency safety comes from ownership and synchronization, not spare capacity. Distinct indexes plus a final join differ from concurrent append.

lessons.title: Shared slices and concurrent append

lessons.explanation:
Reading a key that is absent returns the value type's zero value, with no error. That is why comma-ok exists: v, ok := m[k] distinguishes "absent" from "present and zero".

The asymmetry to remember: reading from a nil map is legal and returns zero values, but writing to one panics. A map must be made before it can be written.
lessons.objective: Use comma-ok, and know which map operation panics.
lessons.title: Reading a missing key is fine, writing to a nil map is not

lessons.explanation:
A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes, commonly containing UTF-8. `s[i]` returns one byte and `len(s)` counts bytes.

Ranging over a string decodes UTF-8 and yields each rune with its byte offset. A rune is a Unicode code point, not necessarily a whole displayed character: combining marks and emoji sequences can contain several code points.
lessons.objective: Index, slice and iterate a string without corrupting characters.
lessons.question: Why do the two lengths differ, and which byte offsets appear?
lessons.title: A string is bytes; range gives you runes

lessons.explanation:
Since Go 1.23, `range` accepts a function as well as a slice, map or channel. A function of the shape `func(yield func(V) bool)` is an iterator: it calls `yield` once per element, and stops early when `yield` returns false — which is how a `break` in the caller's loop reaches you.

There are two shapes, and the standard library names them in `iter`: `iter.Seq[V]` yields one value per step, and `iter.Seq2[K, V]` yields two, which is what map-like iteration needs. You rarely write the type out; you write the function, and `range` accepts it.

The point is not novelty. Before this, a function returning a sequence had to hand back a whole slice — allocating every element even when the caller wanted the first one — or take a callback and lose `break`, `continue` and `return`. An iterator is lazy and keeps the loop keywords working, which is why `slices.Values` and `maps.Keys` return one instead of a copy.
lessons.objective: Write something that can be ranged over without building a slice first.
lessons.title: range works on functions too

lessons.explanation:
A slice has both a length and a capacity, and they gate different things. Indexing is checked against len: `s[i]` panics the moment i reaches len, however much capacity remains behind it. Reslicing is checked against cap: `s[:n]` is legal for any n up to cap, and that is how a slice grows back into space it had already allocated.

This is why `make([]int, 0, 10)` is not indexable at all and `make([]int, 10)` is: the first has room for ten and holds none.
lessons.objective: Say which of two similar-looking index expressions panics.
lessons.question: What does this print?
lessons.title: len is what you may read; cap is what you may reslice

lessons.explanation: Visible length is not retained memory size. A small view can keep an entire allocation reachable. This is often noticed when a parser, cache or queue stores a few bytes from each large input and memory grows far beyond the stored lengths.
lessons.objective: Recognize retained backing arrays and detach small long-lived results deliberately.

sections.body: The function returns only sixteen bytes, but the result still points into the large allocation. As long as that backing array remains reachable, garbage collection cannot reclaim the array just because most of its bytes are outside the returned view.
sections.title: Follow the reference that survives
sections.walkthrough: The 8 MiB allocation is an illustrative size, not a threshold in Go. The problem is the lifetime mismatch: a short prefix outlives the large buffer it views.

sections.body: Copy a small result when it needs an independent lifetime. The copy costs time and an allocation, so use it at a boundary such as inserting into a long-lived cache, not indiscriminately inside every short-lived operation.
sections.title: Detach only what must outlive the input
sections.walkthrough: Clipping capacity with data[:n:n] alone would not detach the original array. Setting one local variable to nil also does not help while another live view still refers to the allocation.

sections.body: Distinguish bytes allocated over time from bytes still live. A temporary copy can increase allocation traffic while reducing retained memory. Inspect heap profiles in the real service, reproduce with representative payloads, and compare before and after. For slices of pointers, discarded elements can also retain pointed-to objects; use appropriate clearing or slices helpers when shrinking reusable storage.
sections.title: Measure retention rather than guessing

reading.takeaway: Optimize lifetimes, not just lengths. A small copy can release a much larger backing array once all other references are gone.

lessons.title: A tiny slice can keep a large buffer alive

lessons.explanation:
The language does not specify map iteration order, and the order may change from one iteration to the next. A small example that repeatedly uses one order does not establish a guarantee.

When output must be deterministic, collect the keys, sort them and read values in that sorted order. When order is irrelevant, test the entries without requiring a particular traversal sequence.
lessons.objective: Produce stable output from a map without hoping.
lessons.title: Map iteration order is not specified

lessons.explanation:
Strings are immutable. Repeated `s += piece` operations in a growing loop can copy the accumulated prefix repeatedly, producing quadratic work as the output grows. Small fixed concatenations may be optimized differently, so measure the actual workload.

`strings.Builder` accumulates text in a growing buffer and exposes the result with `String`. `strings.Join` is a simpler choice when all pieces are already collected. A non-zero Builder must not be copied.
lessons.objective: Use strings.Builder for repeated construction without rebuilding the prefix.
lessons.title: Concatenating in a loop repeatedly rebuilds a string

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Creating a slice with make" page and Effective Go's "Allocation with new" page are the same distinction. `new(T)` allocates a zero T and returns `*T`. That is all it does. `make` is only for slices, maps and channels: it allocates the backing store and returns a usable value, not a pointer to one.

`new(map[string]int)` is a pointer to a nil map. Writing through it panics. `make(map[string]int)` is a map you can write. The same trap exists for a slice: `new([]int)` is `*[]int` pointing at nil; `make([]int, 0, 8)` is a slice with room.
lessons.objective: Pick make or new for a slice, a map and a pointer.
lessons.title: make builds the header; new only allocates

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Arrays" page is the one people skip because slices are what you use. Then a function signature says `[32]byte` and the compiler refuses a `[16]byte`. The length is in the type: `[4]int` and `[3]int` are as different as `int` and `string`.

An array is a value. Assigning it copies every element. A slice is a header pointing at an array, which is why two slices can share memory and two arrays never do unless you pass a pointer. The conversion is one way and explicit: `s := a[:]` views the array; there is no implicit `[n]T` from a slice of the wrong length.
lessons.objective: Write a function that takes [4]int and returns [3]int.
lessons.title: The length is part of an array's type

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Mutating Maps" page is the two-value read: `elem, ok := m[key]`. A missing key and a present zero look the same if you only take `elem`. Scores, counts, flags — anything whose zero is a legitimate stored value — need the ok.

`delete(m, key)` is the other half of that page. Deleting a missing key is a no-op, not an error. After delete, ok is false even if the old value was zero.
lessons.objective: Report whether a key is present when its value can be zero.
lessons.title: Comma-ok is how you tell zero from missing

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Nil slices" page: the zero value of a slice is nil, it has length and capacity 0, and it has no backing array. `append` treats that as a valid empty slice and allocates. JSON encodes a nil slice as `null` and a non-nil empty one as `[]` — the only common place the distinction leaks out.

`s == nil` is true for `var s []int` and false for `s := []int{}`. Both have len 0. Prefer `len(s) == 0` unless you are talking to a wire format that cares.
lessons.objective: Predict what len, == nil and append do to a zero slice.
lessons.question: What does this print?
lessons.title: A nil slice is empty, and append still works

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Function values" page: functions are values. They can be arguments and results. The type includes the parameters and the result, so `func(int) int` and `func(int) string` are as different as int and string.

This is not a method and not a generic yet. It is the shape map and filter had in Go before type parameters, and it is still how most callbacks are written.
lessons.objective: Apply a func(int) int to every element of a slice.
lessons.title: A function is a value you can pass

summary: Length against capacity, shared backing arrays, and why a string is not a []char.
title: Slices, maps and strings
translationNote: This is where habits from Python and JavaScript do real damage. A Go slice is a view over an array, not a list object, so two slices can share memory and a third can silently observe your writes.

lessons.explanation:
A type satisfies an interface by having the methods. There is no implements keyword and no import relationship, so a package can accept types that were written before its interface existed.

The idiom that follows: accept interfaces, return structs. And keep the interface as small as the function actually uses — one method is common and two is already a design decision.
lessons.objective: Write the smallest interface a function needs, at the call site.
lessons.title: The consumer declares the interface

lessons.explanation:
A method with a value receiver belongs to both T and *T. A method with a pointer receiver belongs only to *T.

So if any method that satisfies an interface has a pointer receiver, a plain value does not satisfy it — and the compiler says "does not implement", often pointing at a line that looks obviously correct. The fix is nearly always &value rather than changing the receiver.
lessons.objective: Predict whether a value or only a pointer satisfies an interface.
lessons.question: Why must the assignment use &c, and what does this print?
lessons.title: Pointer receiver, pointer method set

lessons.explanation:
An interface value holds a dynamic type and a dynamic value. It is nil only when it holds neither. Assigning a nil `*MyError` to an `error` variable preserves the pointer type, so `err != nil` is true even though its contained pointer is nil.

When a function returns an error interface, return literal `nil` on the success path rather than a typed nil pointer. Calling a method on an interface holding a nil pointer is safe only if that method deliberately supports a nil receiver.
lessons.objective: Explain why err != nil can be true when the error is nil.
lessons.question: Does this print true or false, and why?
lessons.title: A nil pointer in an interface is not a nil interface

lessons.explanation:
A type assertion has two forms and the difference matters. `v := x.(int)` panics when x is not an int. `v, ok := x.(int)` never panics: ok says whether it worked, and v is the zero value when it did not. In anything that handles input you did not write, the two-value form is the only one.

A type switch is the same question asked about several types at once, and it is how Go writes what other languages do with pattern matching or a visitor.
lessons.objective: Read a value out of an interface without risking a panic.
lessons.title: Asking an interface what it is holding

lessons.explanation:
Writing a type inside a struct without a field name embeds it, and its methods are promoted to the outer type. It looks like inheritance and is not: there is no virtual dispatch and no super. The outer type gets a field it can reach through, and the promoted methods still run against that inner value.

The consequence people trip on: a method the outer type declares shadows the promoted one for outside callers, but a promoted method calling a sibling still calls the inner one. Go resolves this at compile time by name, not at run time by receiver.
lessons.objective: Predict which method runs when an embedded type has one too.
lessons.question: What does this print? Look carefully at the second line.
lessons.title: Embedding is not inheritance

lessons.explanation:
`fmt.Stringer` is a small formatting contract:

```go
type Stringer interface { String() string }
```

Common string formatting operations in `fmt` call `String()` when the value implements it. Format verbs that explicitly request another representation may behave differently. No registration is needed.

Do not format the same value through its own String method in a way that calls String again. Convert it to its underlying type or format its fields to avoid recursion.
lessons.objective: Make a type print itself as a dotted IPv4 address.
lessons.title: fmt looks for String(), not a Stringer keyword

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "The empty interface" page: `interface{}` specifies zero methods, so every type implements it. `any` is the alias. `fmt.Print` takes `...any` for that reason.

Holding a value in `any` throws the static type away. Getting it back is a type assertion or a type switch — the two-value form, or you panic. `%T` in fmt is the cheap way to see what is inside, and it is what this lesson asks you to return.
lessons.objective: Report the dynamic type of a value held in any.
lessons.title: any is interface{}, and it has no methods

summary: Implicit satisfaction, method sets, and the nil that is not nil.
title: Interfaces
translationNote: Nothing declares that it implements an interface. That inverts where abstraction lives: the consumer defines the interface it needs, so the useful interfaces are small and defined next to the code using them, not next to the type satisfying them.

lessons.explanation:
Type parameters go in square brackets before the ordinary ones: `func Map[T, U any](in []T, f func(T) U) []U`. `T` and `U` are types the caller supplies, and in almost every call the compiler infers them so you write `Map(names, length)` with no brackets at all.

`any` is the constraint that allows every type. It is a real alias for `interface{}`, but in this position it means something different: with `interface{}` as a *parameter* type you get a value you must assert your way out of, and with `any` as a *constraint* you get the caller's actual type, checked at compile time.

That is the whole gain. The old version of this function returned `[]interface{}` and every caller unpacked it; the generic one returns `[]U`, and a mistake is a compile error rather than a panic.
lessons.objective: Write a function that works for several types without interface{} and without a cast.
lessons.title: A type parameter is written in square brackets

lessons.explanation:
A constraint says what the compiler may assume about `T`. It is written as an interface — the same keyword — but an interface used as a constraint can list *types* as well as methods:

```
type Number interface {
	~int | ~int64 | ~float64
}
```

The `|` is a union, and the `~` means "any type whose underlying type is this", so `type Celsius float64` satisfies `~float64`. Without the tilde your own named types are excluded, which is almost never what you meant.

The standard library provides `cmp.Ordered` for types that support ordering. `constraints` is not a standard-library package. Reaching for `cmp.Ordered` before writing your own is useful, because a constraint is part of your API and a homemade one is a second vocabulary for readers to learn.
lessons.objective: Constrain a type parameter to what your code actually needs.
lessons.title: A constraint is an interface with types in it

lessons.explanation:
Types take parameters with the same syntax: `type Stack[T any] struct { items []T }`. Methods on it repeat the parameter in the receiver — `func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)` — which makes the type's parameter available to the method.

For most of generics' life a method could not introduce a parameter of its own, so transformations to another type were written as functions before Go 1.27. That restriction is gone; the next lesson is about what replaced it.

The zero value still has to work. `var s Stack[int]` gives you a struct whose slice is nil, and appending to a nil slice is fine, so the stack is usable without a constructor — worth designing for rather than stumbling into.

Instantiation is explicit where inference has nothing to work from: `Stack[int]{}` names the type, while `Push(1)` infers nothing because `T` is already fixed by the receiver.
lessons.objective: Write a container that holds one type rather than any type.
lessons.title: A type can take parameters too

lessons.explanation:
Go 1.27 lets a method declare type parameters of its own, in addition to the ones its receiver already carries:

```
type List[E any] []E

func (l List[E]) Apply[F any](f func(E) F) List[F] {
	...
}
```

`E` comes from the receiver; `F` belongs to the method. Before this, the second one had no place to live, so this transformation was commonly written as a package-level function taking the collection as its first argument. That was not a style choice — the language had no way to write it as a method.

Like a generic function, a generic method is instantiated before it is called, and in ordinary code the compiler infers the type argument from what you pass. The judgement from the previous lessons still applies: this removes a restriction, it does not create an obligation. A method earns a type parameter when the transformation genuinely produces a different element type, and not because it now can have one.
lessons.objective: Write the method that could only be a function before Go 1.27.
lessons.title: A method can take its own type parameter

lessons.explanation:
The Go team's own guidance is narrow. Type parameters are for: functions over slices, maps and channels of any element type; general data structures like trees and stacks; and methods that are identical for several types apart from the type itself.

The case against everything else is readability. A generic function has to be read twice — once for what it does and once for what its constraint permits — and it cannot use anything the constraint does not promise, which usually makes it *less* capable than the concrete version it replaced.

Two smells worth naming. If the constraint ends up being an interface with methods and nothing else, an ordinary interface parameter is simpler and does the same thing at the cost of one dynamic dispatch. And if a function has a type parameter used exactly once, in one argument, it is a plain function wearing a costume.
lessons.objective: Recognise the three cases where a type parameter earns its place, and the ones where it does not.
lessons.question: Both compile and print the same thing. Which should you write, and why?
lessons.title: Most code that could be generic should not be

summary: Type parameters, constraints, and the times an interface is the better answer.
title: Generics, and when not to
translationNote:
If you are coming from Java or C#, the shape will look familiar and the culture will not. Go got type parameters late and on purpose, and the community's default is still to reach for them last — a function that works on one concrete type is not a failure waiting to be generalised.

There is no reflection-based erasure story to learn and no covariance rules to fight. Interfaces describe both ordinary values and type-parameter constraints. A constraint with type terms is not an ordinary value type: use it to bound a type parameter.

lessons.explanation:
fmt.Errorf with %w produces an error that both reads well and still contains the original. errors.Is and errors.As walk that chain.

Two conventions make the chain readable: error strings are lowercase and unpunctuated because they get concatenated, and each layer adds only what it uniquely knows — usually the operation and its input.
lessons.objective: Wrap an error so callers can still match the original.
lessons.title: %w adds context without hiding the cause

lessons.explanation:
errors.Is asks whether anything in the chain equals a sentinel. errors.As asks whether anything in the chain is a particular type, and gives it to you so you can read its fields.

Sentinel when the caller only needs to know which kind of failure it was; typed error when the caller needs a detail, such as which field was invalid.
lessons.objective: Choose between errors.Is and errors.As without trial and error.
lessons.title: Is compares, As extracts

lessons.explanation:
A deferred call runs when the function returns, whichever return it was, and deferred calls run in reverse order. That is what makes acquire-then-defer-release safe against every early return an error check introduces.

The argument to a deferred call is evaluated immediately; only the call is postponed. This surprises people exactly once.
lessons.objective: Release what you acquired, in the right order, on every path.
lessons.question: In what order do the numbers print?
lessons.title: defer runs last in, first out

lessons.explanation:
`error` is an interface with one method, so anything with `Error() string` is one. That is what makes an error able to carry structured information: a field for the line that failed, the value that was rejected, the operation that was attempted.

`errors.As` is the counterpart to `errors.Is`. Where Is asks "is this that particular error", As asks "is there an error of this type anywhere in the chain, and if so give it to me" — which is how a caller reads those fields back out after the error has been wrapped.
lessons.objective: Write an error that carries data the caller can read.
lessons.title: An error is any type with an Error method

lessons.explanation:
A file that will not open is a failure: it is expected, the caller can do something about it, and it is an error value. An index past the end of a slice is a bug: the program's own logic is wrong, and continuing would be worse than stopping. Go draws that line deliberately, and a library that panics on bad input has drawn it in the wrong place.

`recover` exists, and its honest use is narrow: stopping one request from taking down a server, at the boundary, before returning an ordinary error. It is not a catch block, and using it as one hides the bug that caused it.
lessons.objective: Say which of two situations deserves a panic.
lessons.question: What does this print? Note that err is a named return.
lessons.title: panic is for bugs, not for failures

lessons.explanation:
The Tour shows panic as a value and Effective Go keeps recover for a server boundary: one request, one goroutine, then an ordinary error back to the caller. `recover` only works inside a deferred function. A named result is how that error gets out — a `return nil` after `work()` would overwrite it.

A library that recovers in the middle of a calculation is hiding a bug. A process that recovers at main is pretending the program is still sound. The honest width is one unit of work you can abandon.
lessons.objective: Turn a panic into an error without swallowing the rest of the program.
lessons.title: recover belongs at the boundary

summary: Wrapping, errors.Is and errors.As, sentinels, defer and the panic boundary.
title: Errors
translationNote: There is no catch. An error is a value you return, and the caller decides. What replaces a stack trace is a chain of wrapped context, built deliberately at each level that knows something the level below did not.

lessons.explanation:
`go.mod` names the module, such as `example.com/forge`. A package in `internal/build` is then imported using `example.com/forge/internal/build`.

The import path locates the package; its `package` clause determines the default name used in source. The name often matches the last directory component, but does not have to. An import alias can choose another local name.

An `internal` directory also enforces an import boundary: only code within the tree rooted at its parent may import that package.
lessons.objective: Predict the import path of any package in a module.
lessons.question: How does cmd/forge/main.go import Run, and could a different module do the same?
lessons.title: The import path is the module path plus the directory

lessons.explanation:
An identifier starting with an upper-case letter is visible outside its package; anything else is not. There is no public, private or protected.

Because the name carries the visibility, renaming is an API change, and Go's naming conventions get unusually strict: no stuttering (build.Runner, not build.BuildRunner), no Get prefix on getters, and short names for short-lived variables.
lessons.objective: Control visibility without keywords, and name things accordingly.
lessons.title: A capital letter is the access modifier

lessons.explanation:
A test is a function such as `func TestParse(t *testing.T)` in a file ending `_test.go`. It can use the production package name, or a package name ending `_test` to exercise the exported API from outside the package.

A table-driven test keeps cases in data and the assertion in code. `t.Run` gives each case a separate name in the result stream. No external test framework is required.
lessons.objective: Write a table-driven test and run it locally.
lessons.title: Tests are a file, not a framework

lessons.explanation:
A package's name becomes the qualifier callers read: `http.Server` is clearer than `http.HTTPServer`. Prefer short, descriptive lowercase names. Singular names are common, but useful standard-library packages such as `strings`, `errors` and `slices` are plural.

Avoid needless repetition between package and exported name. `chart.New` can be clear for a package centered on one chart type; a package with several constructors may need more specific names. Read the whole selector to judge it.
lessons.objective: Name a package and its exported function without repeating yourself.
lessons.question: What does this print?
lessons.title: The package name is half the API

lessons.explanation:
A package initializes its variables using their dependency relationships, then runs its init functions in source order as presented to the compiler. Imported packages finish initialization before the importing package. `main` starts after the program's initialization completes.

Do not depend on arbitrary file presentation order for important behavior. Explicit constructors make configuration and recoverable failure handling visible. An init function takes no arguments and returns no result, though it can register a driver or format as a deliberate import side effect.
lessons.objective: Predict the order of package variables, init and main.
lessons.question: In what order do the lines appear?
lessons.title: init runs before main, and order is defined

summary: Import paths, go.mod, go test and go vet, without a search engine.
title: Packages, modules and tooling
translationNote: Go's survey found professionals repeatedly returning to documentation for core go subcommands. That is not a knowledge gap so much as a model gap: once the module, the import path and the package directory line up in your head, the commands stop needing to be memorised.

lessons.explanation:
A send on an unbuffered channel does not complete until a receiver takes the value, and a receive does not complete until a sender provides one. It is a rendezvous, not a mailbox.

This is why the classic first Go deadlock is one line long: send on an unbuffered channel from the only goroutine there is, and nobody can ever arrive to meet it. The runtime notices that every goroutine is asleep and stops the program, which is a much better failure than a silent hang.
lessons.objective: Say what blocks, and for how long, on a channel with no buffer.
lessons.question: What happens, and would a buffer of one change it?
lessons.title: An unbuffered channel is a meeting

lessons.explanation:
go f() starts f and immediately continues. There is no future to await and no value to collect, so the result has to come back through a channel or a shared variable protected by something.

The second half matters just as much: when main returns, the program exits and every remaining goroutine simply stops. A goroutine still blocked at that moment did not fail — it was never finished.
lessons.objective: Get a result out of a goroutine, and know when the program stops waiting.
lessons.question: Is the second goroutine guaranteed to print?
lessons.source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	results := make(chan int)
	go func() { results <- 42 }()
	go func() { fmt.Println("this may never print") }()
	fmt.Println(<-results)
}
lessons.title: go returns nothing

lessons.explanation: Starting a goroutine creates an obligation: identify who asks it to stop and who observes that it has stopped. Canceling a context closes a signal; it does not terminate arbitrary Go code. Every blocking point must cooperate or have another bounded exit.
lessons.objective: Design a worker so it can stop waiting and its owner can wait for it to finish.

sections.body: A producer may outlive its consumer. If the consumer returns early, an unconditional send can wait forever and keep its goroutine and reachable objects alive. Select between sending and cancellation.
sections.title: A blocked send needs an escape
sections.walkthrough: If the send and cancellation are both ready, select may choose either. Design the protocol to tolerate that race in intent; cancellation does not mean no operation can ever finish afterwards.

sections.body: A done channel acknowledges exit. The owner cancels, then waits. The worker must observe ctx, including inside downstream operations, or this wait can still block. Production shutdown also needs an overall timeout and a clear policy when a dependency refuses to return.
sections.title: Wait for the owned goroutine
sections.walkthrough: The worker closes done because it owns the completion signal. Do not close a work channel from an unrelated receiver while senders may still use it.

sections.body: For every worker, list start, inputs, outputs, stop signal and join point. Include error paths, not only success. Context does not interrupt a mutex lock or CPU loop automatically; choose primitives and loop checkpoints accordingly. A finalizer or the garbage collector is not a goroutine cleanup strategy.
sections.title: Use a lifecycle checklist

reading.takeaway: Cancellation communicates intent. A join or completion acknowledgement establishes that the owned work has actually stopped.

lessons.title: Cancellation is a request; joining proves exit

lessons.explanation:
Closing a channel says that no more values will be sent. Give that decision to the producer, or to a coordinator that knows all producers have finished. A receiver should not close a stream while senders may still use it.

Receivers can drain a closed buffered channel. `v, ok := <-ch` reports false only when the channel is closed and empty; `for v := range ch` then ends. Sending after close and closing twice both panic.
lessons.objective: Decide who closes a channel, and why the other side must not.
lessons.title: The sender closes, the receiver ranges

lessons.explanation:
select blocks until one of its cases can proceed, and picks randomly among those that are ready. Adding a case for <-ctx.Done() turns any wait into a cancellable one.

The convention that makes this composable: context is the first parameter, it is passed rather than stored, and cancel is always deferred so the resources behind it are released on every path.
lessons.objective: Make a blocking operation cancellable without a flag or a kill switch.
lessons.title: select waits on several things; context says stop

lessons.explanation:
A channel is useful for transferring values and coordinating ownership. A mutex protects shared state that remains in place. Choose the mechanism that makes the invariant and its owner easiest to understand; neither mechanism is always faster.

Keep the mutex next to the data it protects and use the same locking rule for every read and write participating in the invariant. A small, clearly bounded critical section is easier to maintain than a lock whose protected state is scattered.
lessons.objective: Choose between a mutex and a channel for a given problem.
lessons.title: A mutex is for state; a channel is for handing over

lessons.explanation:
A fixed number of workers bounds concurrent processing. The producer sends jobs and closes the input stream after the last job. Workers consume it until it is drained. A coordinator waits for every worker before closing the output stream.

Results may need to be consumed while jobs are still being produced, or backpressure can deadlock the producer and workers. Add cancellation deliberately, and test termination as well as returned values.
lessons.objective: Build a fixed set of workers that finishes cleanly.
lessons.title: The worker pool, written once

lessons.explanation: Concurrency is how work overlaps. Capacity is how much useful work the system can sustain. A thousand waiting goroutines do not give Redis a thousand extra cores or increase a database connection budget. They do consume memory, queue time and cancellation bookkeeping.
lessons.objective: Bound active workers and queued work according to the resource that actually limits throughput.

sections.body: Suppose one downstream operation takes about 20 ms at the target load. Twenty concurrent operations can support roughly 1,000 operations per second in that simplified steady-state example. Real latency distributions, payload size and server limits change the result. Treat it as a sizing hypothesis, then measure tail latency and saturation.
sections.title: Start with a budget

sections.body: A fixed worker count bounds active calls. A bounded jobs channel also bounds queued work. A context-aware producer stops waiting when the request is no longer useful. This fragment shows the admission point; workers, cancellation and channel ownership must all belong to the same enclosing operation.
sections.title: Apply admission control before creating more work
sections.walkthrough: Do not launch a new goroutine for every rejected or blocked enqueue: that merely moves an unbounded queue from the channel into goroutine stacks.

sections.body: For request/response traffic, reject work that cannot meet its deadline or wait only within a bounded budget. For background work, use a durable queue if losing work is unacceptable. A worker pool limits concurrency, not requests per second; add rate limiting when the downstream contract is a rate. Track active calls, queue depth, queue age, errors and latency together.
sections.title: Pick a deliberate overload response

reading.takeaway: Bound workers, waiting work and waiting time. Size those limits from downstream behavior, then verify under load.

lessons.title: More goroutines are not more capacity

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Buffered Channels" page: `make(chan int, 100)` sends without a receiver until the buffer is full, and receives without a sender until it is empty. An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous. A buffered one is a mailbox of a known size.

The deadlock people then write is filling a buffer of 1 with two sends from the only goroutine there is. The buffer does not make the channel unbounded. It makes the bound visible in the `make`.
lessons.objective: Send n values on a channel of capacity n without another goroutine.
lessons.title: A buffer is a mailbox, not a meeting

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Range and Close" page: `v, ok := <-ch` sets ok to false once the channel is closed and empty. `for v := range ch` is that loop written once. Only the sender closes. Sending after a close panics. Closing is not required for the garbage collector — only for telling a range there is nothing more.

Channels are not files. Most of them never close, because nobody is ranging. Close when a range (or an ok-receive) needs the signal.
lessons.objective: Drain a channel with range, and close it from the sender.
lessons.title: range over a channel ends when it closes

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Default Selection" page: a `default` case runs when no other case is ready, so the select returns instead of blocking. That is how you poll a channel, and how you try a send without parking the goroutine.

Without default, select waits. With it, "nothing ready" is a value you handle, not a hang. A busy loop of default-selects is a spin; use it for a single try, not as a substitute for a timer.
lessons.objective: Receive from a channel if a value is ready, and return if it is not.
lessons.title: default makes select try, not wait

lessons.explanation:
The Tour writes `ch <- v` and `v := <-ch` and then, in Effective Go, the type itself carries the arrow: `chan<- int` is send-only, `<-chan int` is receive-only. A function that only produces values should take `chan<- T`. The compiler then refuses a receive in that body, which is the whole point — the restriction is the API.

Conversion is one way: a bidirectional channel may be passed where a directional one is wanted. The other direction does not compile. Close is a send-side operation, so it belongs on `chan<- T`.
lessons.objective: Write a producer that takes chan<- int and closes it.
lessons.title: The arrow in the type is who may send

lessons.explanation:
Effective Go and the sync docs: `Once.Do(f)` runs f once, even when many goroutines call Do at the same time. After that, Do is a no-op. It is the right shape for a lazy setup that must not run twice — registering a driver, reading a config, seeding a generator.

Do not copy an Once after it has been used. Do not call Do with a different f and expect that second f to run. The once is on the Once, not on the function value.
lessons.objective: Initialise shared state without a lock you have to remember.
lessons.title: sync.Once runs a function one time, for everyone

summary: Goroutines, channel ownership, select, buffers and who may send.
title: Concurrency
translationNote: A goroutine is not a promise and not a thread. It has no handle, no return value and no join — which is why channels and WaitGroups exist, and why "who closes this channel" is a design question rather than a detail.

lessons.explanation:
io.Reader has Read. io.Writer has Write. Files, network connections, HTTP bodies, gzip streams, strings.Reader and bytes.Buffer all satisfy one or both.

Accepting them instead of a concrete type is what makes Go code testable without mocks: the test passes a bytes.Buffer and reads the result back.
lessons.objective: Write a function that works on a file, a string and a test buffer.
lessons.title: Two interfaces, one method each

lessons.explanation:
encoding/json maps struct fields by name, and a tag overrides that. Only exported fields are considered, which is the first thing that catches people: a lower-case field is invisible to the encoder with no error.

Unmarshal leaves fields absent from the input untouched rather than zeroing them, so decoding into a reused struct can silently keep old values.
lessons.objective: Control field names, omit empties, and know what unmarshalling leaves untouched.
lessons.question: What is printed, and where did port and secret go?
lessons.title: Struct tags are the JSON schema

lessons.explanation:
`time.Duration` is an int64 counting nanoseconds, and the constants are what make it readable: `5 * time.Second` is a multiplication, not a function call. That is also the trap — a bare `5` is five nanoseconds, and `time.Sleep(5)` requests five nanoseconds, not five seconds. Scheduler timing may make the actual wait longer.

Two more worth knowing on sight: `end.Sub(start)` gives a Duration, and comparing Times uses Before, After and Equal rather than the operators, because a Time carries a monotonic reading as well as a wall clock.
lessons.objective: Write a timeout without wondering what unit it is in.
lessons.question: What does this print? Durations print themselves.
lessons.title: A Duration is a number of nanoseconds with a type

lessons.explanation:
`slices.SortFunc` takes a comparison that returns a negative number, zero or a positive one — not a bool. That trips people coming from languages where the comparator answers "is a before b". `cmp.Compare` does the right thing for any ordered type and is what the comparison should usually be built from.

For a second key, compare the first and fall through only when it is equal. That is the whole pattern, and it is worth writing out once.
lessons.objective: Sort a slice of structs by two keys.
lessons.title: Sorting by whatever you like

lessons.explanation:
A context is how a caller says "stop, I no longer need this". Anything that could block — a network call, a sleep, a channel receive — should take one and should select on `ctx.Done()` alongside whatever it was waiting for. A function that ignores its context is a function nothing can cancel.

`ctx.Err()` says which happened: `context.Canceled` when someone called cancel, `context.DeadlineExceeded` when the timeout ran out. Returning it directly is usually right — the caller already knows what it asked for.
lessons.objective: Make a function that waits stop waiting when told to.
lessons.title: Every blocking call should take a context

lessons.explanation:
Go's own "Writing Web Applications" tutorial and the Tour's "where to go next" both land on `http.Handler`. It is one method:

    ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)

`http.HandlerFunc` turns a function into that type. `http.ServeMux` is a Handler that dispatches to others. The sandbox has no network, so this lesson uses `httptest`: the types are real, the listen is not. A function that accepts `http.Handler` can be tested the same way in any Go module.
lessons.objective: Serve /hello from an in-memory request, with no listen.
lessons.title: http.Handler is one method, like Reader

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's Errors page uses `strconv.Atoi` as the example of a function that returns `(int, error)`. That is the package: no `ParseInt` surprises in everyday code, no `fmt.Sscan` for a single number. `Atoi` is `ParseInt(s, 10, 0)` with a shorter name.

Failure is an error, not a panic and not a zero you are meant to guess at. Discarding that error is how `"x"` becomes port 0.
lessons.objective: Parse a port with Atoi and reject anything outside 1…65535.
lessons.title: strconv is how text becomes a number

lessons.explanation:
`image.Image` describes pixels through three methods: `ColorModel`, `Bounds` and `At`. A decoded PNG produces an image value; the encoded PNG file itself does not implement that interface. A type you write can implement the same pixel contract.

`image/draw` and `image/png` work with image interfaces rather than requiring one concrete bitmap type. This lesson supplies a solid rectangle with chosen bounds and color; encoding that image is a separate step.
lessons.objective: Implement a solid-colour image the standard library will accept.
lessons.title: image.Image is three methods, not a file

summary: io.Reader and io.Writer, encoding/json, and testing without a framework.
title: Standard library patterns
translationNote:
Go's survey lists getting more from the standard library as a top friction. The reason is usually not missing knowledge of a package but missing knowledge of two interfaces: once io.Reader and io.Writer click, a surprising share of third-party code stops being necessary.

Some of this unit runs against in-memory transports rather than real sockets, because the sandbox has no network. The compilation and the types are real; only the transport is simulated, and every lesson says so where it applies.

lessons.explanation: Lifetime is the semantic question: how long must a value remain usable? Stack and heap placement are implementation choices used to satisfy that requirement. The compiler performs escape analysis; source syntax alone is not a dependable allocation profiler.
lessons.objective: Explain why returning a local address is safe and why allocation placement must be measured.

sections.body: Returning a pointer to a local value is normal Go. The implementation arranges storage so callers do not receive a dangling pointer. Do not import C stack-lifetime rules into this code.
sections.title: A local address can safely leave a function
sections.walkthrough: The local spelling c does not disappear in a way that invalidates the returned pointer. Exactly which allocations survive optimization can depend on inlining and the surrounding call sites.

sections.body: A value receiver copies its receiver; a pointer receiver allows shared mutation and may be required by method sets. Neither form is universally faster. Large copies, escaping references, cache locality and synchronization all matter. Start with ownership and API semantics, then inspect a benchmark that represents the actual use.
sections.title: Pointers are a design decision first

sections.body: On a desktop Go installation, compiler diagnostics can report escape decisions. Their wording and decisions can change across versions; they are observations, not API guarantees.
sections.code:
go build -gcflags="-m=2" ./...
go test -bench=. -benchmem ./...
sections.title: Inspect the native build, not an assumption
sections.walkthrough: Use these commands in your development environment. Compare allocations per operation and time after warm-up. The app's WebAssembly sandbox does not reproduce every native service allocation or threading cost.

reading.takeaway: Reason about required lifetime first. Use compiler diagnostics and measurements to learn how the implementation realizes it.

lessons.title: Stacks, escape analysis and object lifetimes

lessons.explanation: Garbage collection reclaims memory that the runtime determines is no longer reachable. It does not know that an application has lost interest in a cache entry, nor does it close a forgotten network connection on a useful schedule. Ownership still matters.
lessons.objective: Follow references from roots and distinguish unreachable objects from unwanted live data.

sections.body: Imagine a global cache holding a pointer to an order, which points to a large receipt buffer. As long as a live reference path reaches the buffer, it is not garbage. Removing one local reference is insufficient when the cache still holds another.
sections.title: Think in reference paths
sections.walkthrough: Delete removes this map entry, not every possible reference to the order. Concurrent access to the map would require synchronization. The example focuses only on the reference graph.

sections.body: An unreachable allocation becomes eligible for reclamation; there is no promise that the operating system immediately receives the same amount of memory. Runtime-managed free space can be reused. RSS, live heap and total allocated bytes answer different questions, so compare like with like when diagnosing growth.
sections.title: Collection is not immediate destruction

sections.body: Close files and response bodies, stop owned background workers, and bound caches according to their contracts. A tracing collector can collect unreachable cycles, but it cannot make an indefinitely blocked goroutine release the values it still reaches. Avoid finalizers as normal cleanup: their timing does not establish a reliable resource protocol.
sections.title: Resources need explicit lifetime management

reading.takeaway: The GC answers reachability, not business usefulness. Remove unwanted references and close resources explicitly; then measure the correct memory metric.

lessons.title: What the garbage collector can and cannot free

lessons.explanation: A service pays for memory in more than one way: live objects occupy space, new allocations create work, and collection uses CPU. Tuning a single GC knob cannot repair an unbounded cache or a queue that retains every request body.
lessons.objective: Distinguish reducing live data from tuning collection frequency and respect a container memory limit.

sections.body: A high allocation rate with a small live heap suggests churn: many objects become garbage quickly. A growing live heap suggests retained data or a growing workload. Capture representative profiles before changing code; removing one temporary allocation is not helpful if a cache retains gigabytes indefinitely.
sections.title: Measure two different problems

sections.body: GOGC influences the heap-growth target and therefore the tradeoff between collection frequency and memory. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft runtime memory limit, not an operating-system hard cap. Native allocations and other process memory can require additional budget. Leave measured headroom under the container limit rather than making the two numbers equal.
sections.code:
# Illustrative native-service configuration, not an iOS setting:
GOGC=100 GOMEMLIMIT=400MiB ./service
sections.title: Treat settings as tradeoffs
sections.walkthrough: The 400 MiB value is an example, not a recommendation for every 512 MiB container. Measure your binary, traffic and non-runtime memory before choosing a value.

sections.body: Avoid retaining whole request graphs in queues, bound cache entries, and reuse buffers only with clear ownership and size limits. Increasing a memory allowance may reduce collection frequency but raises memory use; forcing very frequent GC can waste CPU. A pool is an optimization with lifecycle constraints, not a guarantee that objects will stay cached or that memory use is bounded.
sections.title: Reduce work before aggressive tuning

reading.takeaway: First bound live data and measure allocation churn. Then tune collection within an observed process budget and recheck latency under load.

lessons.title: GC cost, allocation rate and memory budgets

lessons.explanation: A goroutine is a Go execution task scheduled by the runtime. An OS thread is an operating-system execution resource. The runtime multiplexes tasks onto threads; counting goroutines therefore does not tell you how many cores are doing useful work.
lessons.objective: Explain concurrency versus parallel execution without assuming a goroutine is an OS thread.

sections.body: In runtime terminology G represents a goroutine, M an OS thread, and P the scheduler resources needed to execute ordinary Go code. GOMAXPROCS controls how many Ps execute Go code at once. It is not a limit on total goroutines or a universal limit on all process threads.
sections.title: Use the G, M, P model carefully

sections.body: Several CPU-bound tasks need available execution capacity to run in parallel. Waiting network operations can overlap while other work proceeds. Starting ten thousand CPU-heavy goroutines does not create ten thousand cores and may add scheduling overhead. Native defaults can account for runtime and container configuration; inspect the actual service instead of copying a magic setting.
sections.code:
fmt.Println("Go execution slots:", runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0))
fmt.Println("goroutines now:", runtime.NumGoroutine())
sections.title: CPU work and waiting behave differently
sections.walkthrough: Passing zero queries the current GOMAXPROCS value. NumGoroutine is a snapshot and includes runtime/application work; it is a diagnostic signal, not a precise request counter.

sections.body: For CPU work, benchmark a bounded pool around the available CPU budget. For I/O work, use downstream concurrency, queue and deadline limits. A service can be overloaded with many waiting tasks even when CPU looks low. The iOS app's WebAssembly execution environment does not demonstrate native OS-thread behavior; these examples describe native Go services.
sections.title: Choose the right concurrency level

reading.takeaway: Goroutines express concurrency. The runtime and OS determine parallel execution within available CPU and downstream budgets.

lessons.title: Goroutines, OS threads and GOMAXPROCS

lessons.explanation: A rising memory graph is a symptom. Before changing code, ask whether traffic grew, objects are retained, workers are stuck, or allocation churn became expensive. Different diagnostic tools answer different questions.
lessons.objective: Choose a heap profile, goroutine profile, CPU profile or trace to test a specific hypothesis.

sections.body: A heap profile helps find retained allocations; allocation profiles emphasize cumulative allocation traffic. A goroutine profile shows where tasks wait. CPU sampling identifies code consuming CPU, while an execution trace exposes scheduling and blocking relationships. Compare the same workload and interval rather than comparing unrelated snapshots.
sections.title: Choose the observation

sections.body: For a native local program, a goroutine profile can be written to a file without opening an HTTP diagnostics server. Handle the file error and close the file. Profiles can include operational details, so store and share them deliberately.
sections.title: Write a bounded diagnostic capture
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs inside an error-returning diagnostic function and imports os and runtime/pprof. Capture once at the relevant time; do not create an unbounded stream of profile files.

sections.body: If goroutine count grows after requests finish, compare stacks and identify the owner of the repeated wait. If heap grows with cache keys, inspect eviction and reference lifetimes. Change one thing and repeat the workload. A single stable run does not prove absence of races or leaks, and profiling overhead itself should be considered.
sections.title: Turn a suspicion into a comparison

reading.takeaway: Name the hypothesis, choose a tool that can observe it, and compare equivalent workloads before and after the change.

lessons.title: Find a leak by following evidence

title: Runtime and memory
translationNote: Read worked examples without compiling. Native service behavior can differ from the app's WebAssembly execution environment.

lessons.explanation: A Go web service is more than a route callback. Every request consumes a connection, parsing work, application time and possibly downstream capacity. Give those resources explicit lifetimes. This lesson describes native server code; guest Go programs in the app cannot open network sockets.
lessons.objective: Separate request parsing, domain work, downstream deadlines and response writing.

sections.body: A handler translates a protocol into an application operation: validate input, call a service with the request context, then map the result to a response. Domain logic should not need a ResponseWriter. If the client leaves, the request context can notify cooperative downstream work.
sections.title: Keep the boundary small

sections.body: This is a native-server configuration fragment. Header and idle timeouts address specific connection phases; they are not a complete business-operation deadline. WriteTimeout must fit the response type, especially streaming, rather than being copied blindly.
sections.title: Configure a server rather than only a callback
sections.walkthrough: The values are illustrative. Add request-body limits, operation-specific deadlines and response policies based on the API. A timeout does not undo an operation the remote service already committed.

sections.body: HTTP APIs fit request/response interactions and interoperability. A batch program or local library may need no server at all. Test handlers with httptest and in-memory requests before deployment. In-memory handler tests check application behavior; they do not prove production TLS, socket, proxy or load-balancer configuration.
sections.title: Choose HTTP when it matches the problem

reading.takeaway: A handler is an adapter with explicit resource limits. Pass context into the application and test protocol behavior without requiring a running network service.

lessons.title: An HTTP request has a lifecycle and a budget

lessons.explanation: Gin supplies routing, middleware and request/response helpers on top of net/http. It is useful when those conventions reduce repeated adapter code. It does not supply your domain model, persistence policy or downstream capacity, and a small API can also use the standard library.
lessons.objective: Read route groups, path parameters and injected dependencies in a small Gin API.

sections.body: New creates an engine without the default middleware set. The group applies a common path prefix. A named segment is read from the Gin context, then handed to a service. This is an illustrative fragment: store and its result/error contract are application dependencies.
sections.title: Read the route from left to right
sections.walkthrough: This simplified example treats Find failure uniformly. A real adapter should distinguish not-found from timeout, cancellation and internal failure rather than returning 404 for all of them.

sections.body: Construct a handler with the interface it needs, then register methods on the engine. That makes a fake store available to tests and avoids hiding process configuration in globals. Keep route names and response shapes stable as an external contract.
sections.title: Inject the dependency, not a global registry

sections.body: A Gin engine implements http.Handler, so httptest can send an in-memory request through the router and middleware. Assert status, headers and body, including errors. The app includes local-preview patterns, but these reading examples are not a promise that every Gin version or native networking feature runs in its sandbox.
sections.title: Test routing without starting a server

reading.takeaway: Use Gin to express the HTTP adapter. Keep application behavior behind explicit dependencies and test the adapter through its Handler interface.

lessons.title: Gin routes are adapters, not the whole application

lessons.explanation: Decoded JSON is not yet trusted application input. A field can have the right Go type and still violate a business rule. Bound the body, handle decoding failure, then apply domain validation before writing to storage or calling another service.
lessons.objective: Follow JSON binding, size limits, validation and a safe error response.
