sections.body: This adapter accepts a JSON object with a non-empty name. ShouldBindJSON lets the handler choose its error response instead of relying on an automatically written status. The body cap is a policy example and should match the endpoint.
sections.title: Separate decoding from application rules
sections.walkthrough: The generic error avoids echoing an arbitrary decoder message. A production API can map an over-limit body to 413 and expose structured, documented field errors. Decide whether unknown JSON fields should be rejected and configure that policy deliberately.

sections.body: A valid item ID does not prove the requester may access that item. Authenticate the caller, check authorization at the relevant boundary, and keep secrets out of logs and responses. Binding tags check specified shapes; business invariants may require several fields and current state.
sections.title: Validation does not provide authorization

sections.body: Cover missing fields, wrong types, malformed and oversized input, duplicate requests and unexpected fields according to the chosen policy. Specify whether optional zero values differ from missing values. If accepting a command has an external effect, consider an idempotency contract rather than assuming retries are harmless.
sections.title: Test the cases users actually send

reading.takeaway: Decode, validate shape, enforce business rules and authorization, then perform side effects. Each step has a different responsibility.

lessons.title: Validate a request before doing side effects

lessons.explanation: Redis can be overwhelmed by too much work, large payloads, expensive commands or many clients competing for the same resources. Making every slice element a goroutine only moves pressure downstream. Treat the server, the network and the client pool as separate budgets.
lessons.objective: Distinguish client pool limits, request deadlines, rate limits and bounded command batches.

sections.body: A shared client normally reuses connections. Creating a new client for each request defeats that reuse. A connection-pool setting is not automatically a global rate limiter, and waiting for a connection still consumes request time. Exact option semantics depend on the client version; read its production documentation.
sections.title: Understand what a client pool limits

sections.body: This native Go fragment assumes a configured shared go-redis client. Missing keys and infrastructure failures are different cases. The request context carries the parent lifetime; the shorter local timeout bounds this particular operation.
sections.title: Give each operation a bounded lifetime
sections.walkthrough: 150 ms is an example, not a universal Redis timeout. Configure and verify client network timeouts as well; do not assume a context deadline replaces every transport setting.

sections.body: Pipelining can reduce network round trips, but an enormous pipeline can increase queued work and memory. Bound batch size and total payload, avoid broad scans or expensive hot-path commands, and monitor server latency, errors, pool waits and command volume. Test fallback behavior too: when the cache slows, a sudden flood of misses can overload the database behind it.
sections.title: Batch for efficiency without removing limits

reading.takeaway: Limit work before it reaches Redis. A pool, timeout, rate limiter and bounded pipeline solve different parts of the capacity problem.

lessons.title: Redis is fast; its capacity is still finite

lessons.explanation: A cache is often added to reduce load, yet its failure path can multiply load. When a popular key expires, many callers may fetch the same value at once. When a timeout triggers retries at several layers, one user action can become many downstream operations.
lessons.objective: Design a cache-miss path that avoids multiplying identical work and ambiguous retries.

sections.body: singleflight lets concurrent callers for the same key share one in-flight computation. The loader should have an explicit bounded lifetime. In this fragment loadCtx is owned by the service, not borrowed indefinitely from whichever request happened to arrive first.
sections.title: Collapse duplicate work within a process
sections.walkthrough: group is a shared singleflight.Group. This synchronous form waits for the shared result; callers that must independently stop waiting need a cancellation-aware design, for example DoChan with a select. Coalescing is per process, not a distributed lock across replicas.

sections.body: Choose TTLs from the data contract. Jitter can spread expirations, but it does not make stale data acceptable automatically. Serving a stale value may be useful for a catalogue and wrong for an authorization decision. Bound key count and value size, and ensure a miss cannot start unlimited fallback work.
sections.title: Define cache freshness and failure policy

sections.body: Use a small attempt budget, backoff with jitter and an overall deadline. A timed-out write may already have committed, so an automatic retry can duplicate a side effect without an idempotency contract. Coordinate retries at one layer where possible. Record attempts and final outcomes so apparent success does not conceal amplified downstream load.
sections.title: Retry only a retryable, safe operation

reading.takeaway: Coalesce duplicates, bound fallback work and retry under an explicit contract. A faster happy path does not excuse an unbounded failure path.

lessons.title: Cache misses, retries and overload amplification

summary: HTTP, Gin, Redis and the capacity of downstream services.
title: Go services
translationNote: These reading lessons explain native service designs. They do not add guest network sockets or remote services to the iOS sandbox.

lessons.explanation: Go packages provide namespaces and compile-time dependency boundaries. More packages do not automatically create a cleaner design. Start with behavior that changes together, then separate a boundary when it hides an implementation detail or makes a dependency direction clearer.
lessons.objective: Choose cohesive package boundaries and keep concrete dependencies at the edges.

sections.body: A package named orders can expose orders.Service or orders.Create without repeating a business prefix everywhere. A package called utils tends to accumulate unrelated dependencies because its purpose does not constrain what belongs there. Prefer a name that explains why its exported operations belong together.
sections.title: Keep names useful at the call site

sections.body: The application needs the operation Save, not every method of the database client. Define that need near the code that uses it, and inject an implementation when wiring the process.
sections.title: Let the consumer name a small interface
sections.walkthrough: The concrete SQL or Redis adapter can satisfy this interface implicitly. Do not create an interface for every struct by habit; add it where substitution or a stable boundary is useful.

sections.body: HTTP handlers can depend on application operations; those operations should not need a router context. Keep protocol and storage types from spreading through every function. An internal directory can restrict which importers may use a package, but it does not make a design cohesive by itself. Watch for import cycles as a signal that responsibilities may be entangled.
sections.title: Review dependency direction

reading.takeaway: A good boundary reduces what a caller must know. Use cohesive packages and small consumer-owned contracts where they remove real coupling.

lessons.title: Packages follow responsibilities, not a diagram

lessons.explanation: Ports and adapters is a way to keep a use case independent of delivery and infrastructure details. It is useful when one behavior has several entry points or storage implementations. The value comes from dependency direction, not from the number of folders named domain.
lessons.objective: Trace an HTTP adapter through an application operation to a storage port and compare test boundaries.

sections.body: A request body becomes a CreateOrder command. The application validates business rules and calls an OrderStore port. The HTTP adapter translates the outcome back into protocol terms. The storage adapter translates the port operation into its own database protocol. Domain rules do not inspect HTTP headers or SQL row objects.
sections.title: Trace one operation

sections.body: This example is an application fragment. Validation runs before persistence. The error receives operation context while the caller retains access to its cause.
sections.title: Keep orchestration readable
sections.walkthrough: The interface does not define transaction semantics by magic. If creating an order and publishing an event must be atomic, design that consistency boundary explicitly, for example with a database transaction and an outbox.

sections.body: A fake store can test the use case cheaply, but cannot prove that a SQL adapter writes the right schema. Add integration tests for adapters and a smaller number of end-to-end journeys. Keep fakes faithful to important failure contracts, including cancellation and duplicate requests. Avoid adding layers when a small program has no substitution or ownership problem to solve.
sections.title: Test at more than one boundary

reading.takeaway: Use a port to express an application need and an adapter to translate an external mechanism. Verify both the use case and the concrete boundary.

lessons.title: Ports and adapters with a real request

lessons.explanation: Architecture is a choice about boundaries, change and failure. A modular monolith can keep strong internal boundaries with one deployment. Microservices can separate ownership and release schedules, but add remote calls, distributed failures, versioning and operational work.
lessons.objective: Compare a modular monolith, layered design and microservices using concrete operational tradeoffs.

sections.body: A small team sharing one transaction model may benefit from one deployable process with cohesive packages. Separate services become useful when independent scaling, ownership or delivery outweighs coordination costs. A folder named services does not make a monolith distributed, and a network hop does not make a boundary clean.
sections.title: Choose the smallest useful distribution boundary

sections.body: Early returns keep a short function focused on its successful operation. Names should explain domain meaning; return errors at the layer able to add useful context. Avoid a generic helper that hides the important policy decision from its caller.
sections.title: Make the normal path visible
sections.walkthrough: This fragment makes the ordering of policy checks explicit. The real operation still needs an atomicity and idempotency contract if reservation changes external state. Shorter code is not cleaner when it conceals those obligations.

sections.body: Ask whether one business change requires edits across unrelated packages; whether error ownership is clear; whether interfaces have real consumers; and whether tests describe observable behavior instead of private function calls. Keep formatting with gofmt, document surprising contracts, and remove abstractions that do not pay for their indirection. No architecture style eliminates concurrency, capacity or consistency tradeoffs.
sections.title: Use a change-oriented checklist

reading.takeaway: Choose boundaries for real change and ownership needs. Clear names, explicit errors, narrow contracts and behavioral tests matter in every architecture style.

lessons.title: Choose a style; keep the code easy to change

summary: Package boundaries, ports and adapters, and choosing a useful architectural style.
title: Architecture and clean code
translationNote: Start from one request and one reason to change. Architecture is a set of tradeoffs, not a required folder template.

lessons.explanation: A shell starts in a working directory, and relative paths are resolved there. Before building or moving files, establish that location. These exercises use a new scratch directory on your own Mac or Linux machine; no administrator permissions are needed.
lessons.objective: Use pwd, cd, ls, mkdir, cp and mv in a small disposable workspace.

sections.body: pwd prints the working directory; ls -la includes hidden entries and metadata. cd changes this shell, not every terminal. The home shortcut is expanded by the shell, while a quoted path can contain spaces.
sections.code:
pwd
ls -la
cd "$HOME"
pwd
sections.title: Locate the project before changing it
sections.walkthrough: Compare the two pwd results. ls -la may show .git, but that alone does not establish a repository root. Quoting "$HOME" passes a single path, even if it contains spaces.

sections.body: mktemp -d makes a unique scratch directory. mkdir -p creates missing directory components. cp copies bytes; mv changes the path. Keep the original until you have inspected the destination rather than experimenting on project files.
sections.code:
scratch_dir=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$scratch_dir/input" "$scratch_dir/output"
printf "%s\n" "hello Go" > "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt"
cp "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/copy.txt"
mv "$scratch_dir/output/copy.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
cat "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
sections.title: Create and copy a small fixture
sections.walkthrough: The final line prints hello Go. The > operator creates or truncates the named file; it is appropriate here because the fixture is new. The scratch path stays in scratch_dir for the next command.

sections.body: wc -l counts newline-terminated lines, and cmp compares the copied content. rm removes the specifically named fixture files; rmdir removes only empty directories, making an unexpected leftover visible instead of recursively erasing it.
sections.code:
wc -l "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
cmp "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
rm "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
rmdir "$scratch_dir/input" "$scratch_dir/output" "$scratch_dir"
sections.title: Check the result and remove only the fixture
sections.walkthrough: wc should report one line. cmp is silent with status zero for identical files. The cleanup names only files this exercise created; rmdir fails if another file remains, so inspect rather than adding recursive deletion.

reading.takeaway: Start by checking the working directory, quote paths, and verify copied bytes before removing anything. Practice filesystem changes in a named scratch workspace, not in your only project copy.

lessons.title: Bash essentials: navigate, inspect and copy files

lessons.explanation: Most development investigations begin with a filename, a symbol or a short log fragment. Use small commands to narrow the evidence before opening a huge file. The examples assume you are in a trusted Go project and have a text application log named app.log.
lessons.objective: Combine find, grep, head, tail, sort and uniq without hiding their exit behavior.

sections.body: find selects filesystem entries; grep searches text. The quoted pattern *.go is passed to find rather than expanded by Bash. -exec passes each discovered filename as an argument, preserving spaces without parsing the output of ls.
sections.code:
find . -type f -name "*.go"
find . -type f -name "*.go" -exec grep -nH -F "ListenAndServe" {} +
sections.title: Find source files and search their content
sections.walkthrough: The first command lists Go files. The second prints filename, line number and matching text. No matches can produce a nonzero grep status; distinguish that normal search outcome from an unreadable file.

sections.body: head shows the beginning, tail the end, and tail -f follows appended data until Ctrl-C. Bound a first inspection instead of loading a multi-gigabyte file. Filtering stdout does not capture stderr from a program unless you redirect it explicitly.
sections.code:
head -n 10 app.log
tail -n 40 app.log
grep -n -F "timeout" app.log
tail -f app.log
sections.title: Read a bounded part of a log
sections.walkthrough: Stop tail -f with Ctrl-C when you have enough evidence. It does not stop the process writing the log. grep finds the literal timeout string and reports line numbers rather than interpreting it as a regular expression.

sections.body: uniq -c combines adjacent equal lines, so sort first if order does not matter. This simple pipeline counts exact repeated lines; real structured logs often contain a different timestamp per event and need field-aware parsing.
sections.code: grep -F "ERROR" app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 10
sections.title: Count repeated messages with a clear assumption
sections.walkthrough: The result is a frequency list of identical ERROR lines, not an error rate. With pipefail, an early writer can report a broken pipe when head exits; do not reuse a viewing pipeline as an unquestioned CI pass/fail gate.

reading.takeaway: Use find for paths and grep for text; quote patterns and preserve filenames as arguments. Bounded log inspection and explicit pipeline assumptions are more useful than printing every file.

lessons.title: Find code and inspect logs from the command line

lessons.explanation: Bash is useful for connecting build and deployment tools on a developer machine. Go itself does not require Bash, Docker or Kubernetes. Learning their boundaries helps when a Go program becomes part of a service workflow; these commands are reading examples, not app terminal commands.
lessons.objective: Read a small build script without splitting paths or accidentally invoking a shell through Go.

sections.body: Unquoted parameter expansion can perform word splitting and filename expansion. Quote a variable when its value should be one argument. In Bash, an array preserves several arguments without rebuilding a shell command string.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
project_dir="${1:-.}"
args=(-C "$project_dir" test ./...)
go "${args[@]}"
sections.title: Preserve a path as one argument
sections.walkthrough: With a directory containing spaces, the array still supplies one directory argument. The script uses Bash-specific array syntax; it is not a portable /bin/sh script. The -C option changes Go's working directory before running the command.

sections.body: When a Go process starts a tool, exec.Command passes an argument vector directly. This avoids asking a shell to reinterpret semicolons, substitutions or spaces. It does not by itself make the target command safe; validate its allowed operation and arguments.
sections.title: Keep data out of shell syntax
sections.walkthrough: This is native Go code for a development tool. It does not add subprocess execution to the iOS sandbox. Avoid sh -c with concatenated user input.

sections.body: A few fixed tool invocations can remain a script. Structured retries, complex state, concurrent work and testable domain rules often belong in Go. Quote "$@" when forwarding original arguments, avoid eval, and handle the exit status at the point where failure changes the workflow.
sections.title: Choose Go when the script stops being glue

reading.takeaway: Preserve argument boundaries. Use Bash for small orchestration and direct process argument vectors from native Go when no shell language is needed.

lessons.title: Bash passes arguments; quoting defines their boundaries

lessons.explanation: A script is another program with success and failure paths. A command printing plausible output can still fail. Pipelines complicate this because the last command can succeed even when an earlier producer failed.
lessons.objective: Read pipeline failure behavior and keep configuration and secrets out of command strings.

sections.body: Bash pipefail makes a pipeline fail when a component fails, instead of using only the final command's status. Check that status explicitly at the workflow boundary. set -e has exceptions in conditionals and other constructs, so it is not a replacement for understanding control flow.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u -o pipefail
if go test ./... | tee test.log; then
    printf "%s\n" "Tests passed"
else
    printf "%s\n" "Tests failed; inspect test.log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sections.title: Observe the whole pipeline
sections.walkthrough: tee preserves a log while showing output. With pipefail, a failing go test makes the condition fail even when tee succeeds. This script is for a trusted local project and writes one named log file.

sections.body: A prefix assignment belongs to one child process; export passes a variable to later children from this shell. Check selected non-secret settings instead of dumping the full environment. Already-running services keep their original environment.
sections.code:
APP_ENV=development go run ./cmd/api
export APP_ENV=development
printf "APP_ENV=%s\n" "$APP_ENV"
command -v go
sections.title: Pass configuration and inspect one setting
sections.walkthrough: The first line runs a foreground API until you stop it; execute the following commands after it exits or in another shell. The example assumes cmd/api exists and does not require a credential. command -v shows which Go executable Bash will resolve.

sections.body: A trap can arrange cleanup of resources a script created, but it cannot roll back an external side effect automatically. Avoid rerunning a deployment simply because its status command timed out. Keep a stable operation identifier and inspect the outcome before retrying. As a script grows, move complex state transitions into a program with tests.
sections.title: Make cleanup and retries deliberate

reading.takeaway: A successful last pipeline command does not prove upstream success. Preserve exit status, handle failure explicitly, and avoid exposing configuration secrets.

lessons.title: Pipelines, exit codes and explicit failure handling

lessons.explanation: A process has a PID, an exit status and open streams. Starting a service in the background does not detach it from responsibility: keep the PID and wait for completion. These commands assume a local Go project with cmd/api and an available port.
lessons.objective: Start one Go service, retain its PID, send TERM and wait for its result.

sections.body: Build first, then run the binary itself in the background. $! is the PID of the latest asynchronous command. A background go run process may introduce a build/launcher process, so it is a poor substitute when practicing exact signal ownership.
sections.code:
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/api ./cmd/api
./bin/api > api.log 2>&1 &
api_pid=$!
printf "API PID: %s\n" "$api_pid"
sections.title: Start the binary you can stop directly
sections.walkthrough: Run the launch only after the build succeeds. Both output streams go to api.log. Record this PID instead of searching all processes by a broad application name or terminating unrelated Go jobs.

sections.body: ps reports process state; kill -0 checks that a PID can be addressed without sending a signal. lsof is a separately installed utility on some systems and can identify a listening socket; it does not prove the HTTP handler returns useful responses.
sections.code:
ps -p "$api_pid" -o pid,etime,args
kill -0 "$api_pid"
lsof -nP -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN
sections.title: Inspect the process and the listening port
sections.walkthrough: Check that the socket belongs to the binary you launched. If lsof is missing, use your OS socket inspection tool. A process may exit between any two commands; observation is not a lifetime guarantee.

sections.body: TERM lets a cooperative service drain work. wait observes your shell child and reaps it; an if branch can preserve nonzero status without aborting the shell. SIGKILL prevents application cleanup, so use it only after diagnosing an unresponsive process.
sections.code:
kill -TERM "$api_pid"
if wait "$api_pid"; then
    printf "%s\n" "Service exited successfully"
else
    status=$?
    printf "Service exit status: %s\n" "$status"
fi
tail -n 20 api.log
sections.title: Request shutdown and collect the outcome
sections.walkthrough: A graceful service can return zero. A process terminated by a signal may report a nonzero status; inspect its log and shutdown contract. wait works for children of this shell, not any arbitrary PID from another terminal.

reading.takeaway: Keep the child PID, inspect it, request TERM and wait for the outcome. A listening port, a live process and a successful HTTP response are three different observations.

lessons.title: Processes, signals and exit status

lessons.explanation: A useful script has explicit inputs and predictable cleanup. Bash distinguishes positional arguments, shell variables and exported environment. This lesson puts those pieces into a small test wrapper instead of assuming that adding set -e makes every failure path correct.
lessons.objective: Read required configuration, forward quoted arguments and clean a temporary workspace with a trap.

sections.body: ${1:-.} supplies a default when the first argument is absent or empty. A prefix assignment affects one command environment; export affects later child processes from this shell. Neither changes an already running service.
sections.code:
project_dir="${1:-.}"
printf "Testing: %s\n" "$project_dir"
GOMAXPROCS=2 go -C "$project_dir" test ./...
export APP_ENV=development
printf "APP_ENV=%s\n" "$APP_ENV"
sections.title: Read arguments and pass a setting to one process
sections.walkthrough: The Go -C flag precedes the test command. The temporary GOMAXPROCS assignment does not permanently change your shell. Never print the complete environment to diagnose one non-secret setting.

sections.body: The : command with ${name:?message} reports a required input. mktemp creates the workspace, and EXIT runs cleanup on ordinary shell termination. The script forwards "$@" as separate arguments and uses an explicit test branch to preserve failure.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
: "${PROJECT_DIR:?Set PROJECT_DIR to a Go project}"
work_dir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f "$work_dir/test.log"; rmdir "$work_dir"' EXIT
if go -C "$PROJECT_DIR" test "$@" ./... > "$work_dir/test.log" 2>&1; then
    cat "$work_dir/test.log"
else
    cat "$work_dir/test.log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sections.title: Validate inputs and clean only owned temporary data
sections.walkthrough: Save this as check.sh and call it with bash, PROJECT_DIR set, and optional go test flags such as -count=1. The trap names the one file it owns. SIGKILL and machine failure cannot run shell cleanup.

sections.body: bash -n parses without executing the script; it does not prove that command names, paths or remote systems exist. --help or command -v can establish what is installed. Review changes before making a script executable or putting it into CI.
sections.code:
bash -n check.sh
command -v bash
command -v go
PROJECT_DIR="$PWD" bash check.sh -count=1
sections.title: Check syntax before running the script
sections.walkthrough: Syntax success is silent. The final line runs tests and can download required Go modules; it is an execution step, not another parser check. Keep credentials out of arguments and traces such as bash -x.

reading.takeaway: A script should declare its inputs, preserve argument boundaries and clean only resources it created. Parsing, executing and validating its external effects are separate checks.

lessons.title: Small scripts: arguments, environment and cleanup

lessons.explanation: Git records snapshots, not a magic backup of every unsaved editor buffer. Start in an existing local repository and inspect your changes. The sequence below makes a topic branch, stages one reviewed path and records a local commit; publishing comes in the next lesson.
lessons.objective: Keep working tree, staging area and committed history distinct.

sections.body: git status --short summarizes tracked and untracked paths. git diff shows unstaged tracked changes; git diff --staged shows what the next commit contains. Untracked file content is not included in ordinary git diff.
sections.code:
git status --short
git diff -- main.go
git diff --staged
git log -5 --oneline
sections.title: Inspect before selecting a change
sections.walkthrough: Compare the two diff views. A file can have both staged and unstaged edits, and the next commit includes only the staged snapshot. -- separates options/revisions from the path main.go.

sections.body: switch -c creates and selects a new branch at the current commit. add stages the named content. Inspect the staged result before committing, rather than using add . when a repository includes unrelated experiments or local credentials.
sections.code:
git switch -c feature/health-check
git add -- main.go
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add health endpoint"
sections.title: Put a reviewed change on a topic branch
sections.walkthrough: Use an unused branch name and a real main.go change. The commit remains local until you push it. If a hook fails, inspect its output and rerun the necessary check rather than bypassing it automatically.

sections.body: restore --staged changes the index back toward HEAD while leaving the working file intact. A plain restore of the working tree has a different, destructive meaning. Check both views after unstaging to make the distinction visible.
sections.code:
git restore --staged -- main.go
git status --short
git diff -- main.go
sections.title: Unstage without discarding your edit
sections.walkthrough: Use this on a staged change before committing. Your edits should now be unstaged. This is not a command to undo an existing commit; history repair and reverting a published change are different operations.

reading.takeaway: Review unstaged and staged diffs separately, stage intended paths and commit on a named branch. Unstaging an edit preserves it; overwriting the working tree may discard it.

lessons.title: Git daily work: inspect, branch, stage and commit

lessons.explanation: A remote-tracking branch is your local record of a remote branch at the last fetch. Fetching updates that record without integrating it into your current branch. The examples assume an origin remote, a main branch and an existing topic branch you own.
lessons.objective: Inspect upstream changes before integration and keep unfinished work recoverable.

sections.body: remote -v shows fetch and push destinations; inspect those before publishing. fetch origin updates remote-tracking references. The three-dot diff compares the topic branch against its merge base with origin/main, highlighting the branch contribution.
sections.code:
git remote -v
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
git diff origin/main...HEAD
sections.title: Fetch and compare before merging
sections.walkthrough: HEAD..origin/main lists commits reachable from origin/main but not HEAD. Fetch does not change your working files. A remote URL may contain sensitive information; avoid pasting it indiscriminately into public logs.

sections.body: stash push -u includes untracked files as well as tracked edits, but not ignored files by default. apply restores a stash while retaining its saved entry. Inspect and resolve any conflicts before deciding to drop the saved copy.
sections.code:
git stash push -u -m "WIP before syncing"
git stash list
git stash show --stat "stash@{0}"
git stash apply "stash@{0}"
git status --short
sections.title: Temporarily store an unfinished tracked change
sections.walkthrough: Only apply when a stash entry actually exists. apply can conflict; it does not mean every file was restored cleanly. The retained stash is useful until the restored work is checked. A stash is local, not a shared backup.

sections.body: On a clean main branch, pull --ff-only refuses an implicit merge when histories diverge. A topic branch push sets its upstream without rewriting remote history. A rejected push is evidence to fetch and inspect, not a reason to force-push blindly.
sections.code:
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch feature/health-check
git push -u origin feature/health-check
sections.title: Integrate deliberately and publish the branch
sections.walkthrough: Resolve or save local changes before switching branches. The pull updates main only if fast-forward is possible. Pushing the topic branch publishes commits; it does not merge them into main or submit an application release.

reading.takeaway: Fetch and compare before integrating. Preserve unfinished work, inspect conflicts and push the intended branch. Fast-forward refusal is a useful signal that history needs a deliberate decision.

lessons.title: Git collaboration: fetch, compare, stash and push

lessons.explanation: A useful Go development loop checks the module boundary, formatting, tests, static diagnostics and the final build. These commands are for the native Go toolchain on a development machine; platform support and build tags can change which packages are selected.
lessons.objective: Use the native Go CLI to inspect a module and check a service before packaging it.

sections.body: go version identifies the toolchain. go env GOMOD GOWORK prints selected module/workspace files without dumping every environment setting. list -m all describes the selected build list; mod why explains why a dependency is needed.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -m all
go mod why -m golang.org/x/sync
sections.title: Locate the module and inspect dependencies
sections.walkthrough: Run inside your module; the selected module file should be the one you expect. The last dependency is an example: if it is not required, Go explains that. Module commands may access the configured proxy and network.

sections.body: gofmt -l lists formatting differences without rewriting files. test checks packages; -race adds supported native race instrumentation. vet reports suspicious constructs rather than proving semantic correctness. A clean run still depends on meaningful tests.
sections.code:
gofmt -l .
go test ./...
go test -race ./...
go vet ./...
sections.title: Format, test and inspect suspicious code
sections.walkthrough: Run each check and inspect its status. Race detection needs a supported native platform/toolchain and may require cgo; it is not available through every cross-compilation target. A race-free test run covers only paths actually exercised.

sections.body: mod tidy can add or remove module requirements and sums, so review its diff rather than running it as an invisible deployment step. build -trimpath removes local filesystem paths from the executable; version -m inspects embedded build/module metadata.
sections.code:
go mod tidy
git diff -- go.mod go.sum
mkdir -p bin
go build -trimpath -o ./bin/api ./cmd/api
go version -m ./bin/api
sections.title: Tidy deliberately and inspect the shipped binary
sections.walkthrough: The example assumes cmd/api exists. Test any module file changes before committing. Embedded build metadata is useful for provenance, but build flags and source state must still be recorded for reproducible releases.

reading.takeaway: Check the selected module, format, test, race-check where supported, run vet and inspect the final artifact. Review dependency-file changes explicitly instead of treating tidy as a harmless read-only command.

lessons.title: Go toolbelt: modules, tests, vet and build

lessons.explanation: An API can fail before any handler runs, or return an HTTP error over a perfectly healthy connection. curl helps identify that boundary. These examples target your own local Go service at 127.0.0.1:8080 with a /healthz endpoint; adjust the paths to your application.
lessons.objective: Probe a local API and separate DNS, connection, HTTP and application failures.

sections.body: -i includes response headers, --connect-timeout bounds connection establishment, and --max-time bounds the total operation. --fail-with-body makes HTTP 4xx/5xx nonzero while retaining the response body, unlike an ordinary successful curl transport.
sections.code:
curl -i --connect-timeout 2 --max-time 5 \
  --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.title: Inspect headers and keep a timeout
sections.walkthrough: Expect a successful health response from your server. Connection refused means no reachable listener at that address, not an HTTP 500. A timeout has a different cause again; retain the specific diagnostic instead of reducing all failures to unavailable.

sections.body: --data-binary sends the provided bytes. The content type declares JSON, but the server still has to validate fields. This request is an example for a local /notes route accepting a text field; it is not an endpoint supplied by every Go service.
sections.code:
curl -i --max-time 5 --fail-with-body \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary '{"text":"inspect this request"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/notes
sections.title: Send JSON without hiding the request contract
sections.walkthrough: The single quotes keep Bash from interpreting the JSON double quotes. Data selects POST by default. Do not add a production authorization token to a shared example, shell history or a screenshot.

sections.body: --write-out prints transport timing after the request; -o /dev/null discards the body in this diagnostic. An HTTP status of 000 is not a server status: no HTTP response was received. Inspect hostname resolution separately when using a domain.
sections.code:
curl -sS -o /dev/null --max-time 5 \
  -w 'status=%{http_code} connect=%{time_connect}s total=%{time_total}s\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.title: Measure and reason about the failed layer
sections.walkthrough: This timing command does not use --fail-with-body, so an HTTP 500 can still have curl status zero. Check both the printed HTTP status and the process outcome. Avoid -k as a default fix for TLS errors; correct the hostname and trust configuration.

reading.takeaway: Check transport errors, HTTP status and response body separately. Bound diagnostic requests and preserve the failed layer before deciding whether the problem is routing, TLS, a handler or a downstream dependency.

lessons.title: HTTP debugging: curl, status codes and time budgets

lessons.explanation: A native Go binary can run directly under a service manager; Kubernetes is not required. These examples assume Linux with systemd and a preinstalled go-api.service. They do not apply to macOS launchd or every container environment.
lessons.objective: Inspect a systemd service, follow its logs and understand its restart boundary.

sections.body: systemctl cat shows the installed unit and drop-ins. status includes active state and recent log context; show exposes selected properties. Verify the executable and service user before changing the process lifecycle.
sections.code:
systemctl cat go-api.service
systemctl status go-api.service --no-pager
systemctl show go-api.service -p MainPID -p ActiveState -p SubState
sections.title: Read the unit and its current state
sections.walkthrough: An inactive or failed status can produce a nonzero exit code. Check ExecStart, WorkingDirectory and User in the unit. Unit content may reveal configuration paths; inspect only the required evidence before sharing logs.

sections.body: journalctl selects journal entries for a unit and time range. -f follows new entries; Ctrl-C stops following without stopping the service. Access may require membership or administrator permissions depending on the host configuration.
sections.code:
journalctl -u go-api.service --since "10 minutes ago" --no-pager
journalctl -u go-api.service -n 50 --no-pager
journalctl -u go-api.service -f
sections.title: Follow the unit log instead of guessing a file path
sections.walkthrough: Correlate startup, request errors and shutdown timestamps. A missing journal permission is different from no application logs. The program should emit useful stdout/stderr records without credentials or full sensitive request payloads.

sections.body: daemon-reload reloads unit definitions after editing them; it does not restart a process by itself. restart replaces the running service and can interrupt traffic. An ordinary deployment needs a deliberate change window and an application shutdown budget.
sections.code:
# After an intentional unit-file change on your own host:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart go-api.service
systemctl is-active go-api.service
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.title: Restart the intended service and verify recovery
sections.walkthrough: These two sudo commands mutate host state and need authorization on that machine. Verify both service state and HTTP behavior. A running process can still be unhealthy; repeated restarts can conceal a bad configuration instead of repairing it.

reading.takeaway: Inspect the unit, state and journal before restarting. Reloading definitions and replacing a process are distinct actions; verify the application endpoint after a controlled service change.

lessons.title: A Go service on Linux: systemctl and journalctl

summary: Bash, Git, Go tools, HTTP debugging and Linux service commands.
title: Around Go: command line
translationNote: Read commands and manifests here; use your own development environment to run them. These tools are useful deployment options, not prerequisites for every Go program.

lessons.explanation: A container image packages a native application and its runtime files. It does not compile Go inside the iOS app, and it does not remove the need to maintain the operating environment. Multi-stage builds let the final image omit the compiler and source tree.
lessons.objective: Separate the build stage from the runtime image and identify what a minimal image leaves out.

sections.body: The builder resolves dependencies and compiles a Linux binary. The final stage copies only the program. This example assumes go.mod and go.sum exist and the program lives in cmd/api.
sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
USER 65532:65532
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
sections.title: Read the two stages
sections.walkthrough: This scratch example fits a compatible pure-Go binary with no required external files. It omits CA certificates, zoneinfo, a shell and writable application directories. Add the actual runtime assets or choose an appropriate maintained runtime base. Pin and update base image digests in a reproducible release process.

sections.body: Keep logs, local builds and secrets out of the build context with .dockerignore. Copy module files before source to reuse dependency work. The actual final image still needs a startup test; metadata inspection alone cannot prove its runtime files are sufficient.
sections.code:
docker build -t go-api:dev .
docker image inspect go-api:dev --format '{{.Config.User}} {{json .Config.Entrypoint}}'
docker image ls go-api
sections.title: Build the final image and inspect its metadata
sections.walkthrough: For this Dockerfile the user should be 65532:65532 and the entrypoint /api. Verify the build succeeds before inspecting the tag, or you might inspect an older image. A CGO-dependent program needs a compatible build/runtime strategy.

sections.body: A non-root user reduces ordinary process privileges, but does not replace resource and filesystem limits. Test startup, configuration, TLS requirements and graceful termination using the actual final image. A compiler-stage unit test alone cannot prove the minimal runtime image contains the files the service needs.
sections.title: Run the artifact you intend to release

reading.takeaway: Build with the toolchain, run with the required runtime files, and verify the final image. A smaller image must still satisfy the program's contract.

lessons.title: Build a small Go image with explicit runtime needs

lessons.explanation: Start with a trusted project containing the Dockerfile from the earlier lesson and a Go service listening on :8080. The following commands use an isolated development container named go-api-dev; an image, a container instance and a published port are different objects.
lessons.objective: Run a named local container and diagnose it with logs, inspect and stats.

sections.body: build tags the image produced from the current context. run creates a container; -d runs it in the background and -p publishes a container port at a host address. Bind the host side to loopback when the exercise should stay local.
sections.code:
docker build -t go-api:dev .
docker run -d --name go-api-dev \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 -e APP_ENV=development go-api:dev
docker ps --filter name=go-api-dev
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.title: Build once and start a named instance
sections.walkthrough: Run only after the build succeeds and choose another name or port if already used. The Go listener must accept container-interface traffic, usually :8080. EXPOSE in the Dockerfile alone does not publish anything on the host.

sections.body: logs reads stdout/stderr, inspect can select one property, and stats reports current resource usage. docker exec starts a new command inside the container; a scratch image has no sh, ls or other debugging utility unless you explicitly supplied one.
sections.code:
docker logs --tail 50 go-api-dev
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' go-api-dev
docker stats --no-stream go-api-dev
sections.title: Inspect the instance and its actual runtime
sections.walkthrough: A stopped container is omitted by ordinary ps; use docker ps -a when investigating an exit. ExitCode is not an HTTP status. Avoid dumping all inspect properties when only state is needed because configuration can include sensitive environment data.

sections.body: stop sends a graceful termination signal and allows a finite timeout before forced termination. rm removes the stopped container, not the image or unrelated volumes. Replacing an image tag does not upgrade a previously created container.
sections.code:
docker stop --timeout 15 go-api-dev
docker ps -a --filter name=go-api-dev
docker rm go-api-dev
docker image inspect go-api:dev --format '{{.Id}}'
sections.title: Stop and remove only this instance
sections.walkthrough: Confirm you no longer need the disposable instance before removing it. Persistent state belongs in deliberate storage; removing the container should not be your only backup strategy. Keep the image if you want to reproduce its startup.

reading.takeaway: Build an artifact, create a named instance and verify it through the published port. Inspect its own logs and exit state, then stop it deliberately; image tags and container instances have separate lifecycles.

lessons.title: Docker daily commands: build, run, inspect and stop

lessons.explanation: Compose defines a local multi-container environment in one file. This example assumes your API reads REDIS_ADDR, listens on :8080 and tolerates transient downstream failures. Use a disposable directory for the exercise and save the file below as compose.yaml.
lessons.objective: Read compose.yaml and use config, up, ps, logs, exec and down.

sections.body: Service names provide network discovery on the Compose network. The API connects to redis:6379, not its own localhost. A dependency health check orders initial startup; it does not guarantee Redis stays healthy, so the Go client still needs deadlines and recovery.
sections.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:8080:8080"]
    environment:
      REDIS_ADDR: redis:6379
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
sections.title: Describe services and readiness in the file
sections.walkthrough: This intentionally disposable Redis has no persistent volume or public port. Choose a supported tested image version for your project and pin release digests when needed. The API Dockerfile must exist in the same build context.

sections.body: -p gives the stack a predictable project name. config --quiet validates without printing resolved configuration. up --build -d builds and starts; ps and logs reveal readiness and startup errors. Use the same project name for each command.
sections.code:
docker compose -p go-lab config --quiet
docker compose -p go-lab up --build -d
docker compose -p go-lab ps
docker compose -p go-lab logs --tail 50 api redis
sections.title: Validate, start and inspect the project
sections.walkthrough: Configuration validation does not prove the images will build or the service will boot. A missing Dockerfile, unavailable image or failing Redis health check each needs its own fix. Avoid publishing the full resolved config if it includes secrets.

sections.body: exec runs inside an existing service container; redis-cli PING checks the Redis protocol path. down stops and removes the project containers and its normal networks. It does not delete named volumes unless requested with an additional destructive option.
sections.code:
docker compose -p go-lab exec redis redis-cli PING
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
docker compose -p go-lab down
sections.title: Probe a dependency and tear down deliberately
sections.walkthrough: PING should return PONG, while the HTTP check verifies your API route. Run down only when the local session is finished. This fixture uses ephemeral Redis storage, so its data goes away with the disposable container.

reading.takeaway: Use service DNS names inside a Compose network, validate the file and inspect each service. Initial dependency ordering complements application retry/deadline behavior; it does not replace it.

lessons.title: Compose: run an API and Redis as one local stack

lessons.explanation: A container writable layer usually disappears when its instance is removed. A bind mount maps a host path; a named volume has a lifecycle managed by the container runtime. These local examples use a dedicated fixture and Redis to demonstrate the difference.
lessons.objective: Choose a mount for configuration or persistent state and inspect it without deleting data.

sections.body: A bind mount exposes a host path to the container. --mount makes source, destination and read-only intent explicit. The example assumes ./config.json already exists and the API accepts a -config flag; adapt that flag to your own program.
sections.code:
docker run --rm --name go-api-config \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/config.json,target=/etc/go-api/config.json,readonly" \
  go-api:dev -config /etc/go-api/config.json
sections.title: Mount a configuration file read-only
sections.walkthrough: Unlike some -v forms, --mount reports a missing source instead of silently making a directory. The image must let its configured user read the file. On macOS, file sharing also crosses the container VM boundary.

sections.body: Create a dedicated named volume and mount it at Redis data storage. Append-only persistence records writes into that volume; it does not create an off-host backup. The port remains private to this container unless you publish it separately.
sections.code:
docker volume create go-lab-data
docker run -d --name go-lab-redis \
  --mount type=volume,source=go-lab-data,target=/data \
  redis:8-alpine redis-server --appendonly yes
docker exec go-lab-redis redis-cli SET example hello
sections.title: Give disposable Redis a separate data volume
sections.walkthrough: Use an unused container name. SET changes only this exercise Redis key. The volume survives removal of the container; persistence and restore procedures still need testing against the selected Redis version.

sections.body: Inspect mounts to confirm storage identity, then stop and remove only the Redis instance. The volume remains available for a later explicitly configured container. Avoid prune or rm -v as a casual repair for a service that owns important state.
sections.code:
docker inspect --format '{{json .Mounts}}' go-lab-redis
docker stop go-lab-redis
docker rm go-lab-redis
docker volume inspect go-lab-data
sections.title: Remove an instance without deleting its stored data
sections.walkthrough: The final command should still find the named volume. A missing container is expected after rm. Delete the exercise volume later only when you intentionally no longer need its data and have checked its exact name.

reading.takeaway: Container replacement, volume deletion and backup are separate operations. Use explicit mount paths, account for the service UID and verify storage identity before changing the lifecycle of stateful workloads.

lessons.title: Container storage: bind mounts, volumes and permissions

lessons.explanation: Docker and Podman can build and run OCI-style container images, but their host integration, daemon model, networking and rootless behavior are not identical. An image is an artifact; a container is a running or stopped instance with its own lifecycle.
lessons.objective: Distinguish image, container, host networking and persistent data while comparing local runtimes.

sections.body: These Podman commands build an image from a trusted project and start one named container. The published port is restricted to the local host in this development example. Docker has similar basic commands, but do not assume every option and host behavior is interchangeable.
sections.code:
podman build -t localhost/go-api:dev .
podman run --rm --name go-api \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 localhost/go-api:dev
sections.title: Read build and run separately
sections.walkthrough: The application inside the container must listen on an appropriate container interface, usually :8080, for port forwarding to reach it. Its own localhost is not the host's localhost. --rm removes this disposable container on exit; it does not manage external persistent data.

sections.body: Podman info reports the active environment; select only the rootless field when that is what you need. On macOS and Windows, Podman commonly uses a Linux VM. machine list and machine start manage that VM rather than the individual application container.
sections.code:
podman info --format '{{.Host.Security.Rootless}}'
# On macOS/Windows with an existing Podman machine:
podman machine list
# Start the chosen existing machine only if it is stopped:
podman machine start
sections.title: Inspect rootless runtime and the container VM
sections.walkthrough: Linux installations may not use a Podman machine at all. Rootless does not mean unlimited host access or identical Docker networking. Inspect the selected connection and VM state before creating or restarting any shared environment.

sections.body: Run these in a second terminal while the earlier foreground go-api container is running. logs reads its stdout/stderr, ps selects its state and stop requests graceful termination. The earlier --rm option removes the disposable container on exit.
sections.code:
podman ps --filter name=go-api
podman logs --tail 50 go-api
podman stats --no-stream go-api
podman stop --time 15 go-api
sections.title: Inspect logs and stop the intended instance
sections.walkthrough: Use the exact exercise name so another service is not affected. Persistent data needs a deliberate volume and backup policy; --rm concerns the container instance, not an automatic external-storage lifecycle. The image remains available afterwards.

reading.takeaway: Images, instances, virtual-machine integration and persistent data are different layers. Similar command names do not establish identical runtime behavior.

lessons.title: Docker and Podman: images are not running containers

lessons.explanation: A cluster pulls an image from a registry it can reach; a local Docker image does not appear there automatically. Tags are mutable names, while a digest identifies specific image content. Replace the example registry and owner with a namespace where you have permission to publish.
lessons.objective: Tag and push an image you own, inspect its digest and match its platform to the deployment.

sections.body: Use the registry credential flow appropriate to the host; --password-stdin keeps the token out of process arguments. This example reads a token interactively in Bash, passes it through stdin and unsets the variable after login.
sections.code:
registry=registry.example.com
read -r -s -p "Registry token: " registry_token
printf "\n"
printf "%s" "$registry_token" | docker login "$registry" \
  --username YOUR_USER --password-stdin
unset registry_token
sections.title: Authenticate without a password in the command line
sections.walkthrough: registry.example.com and YOUR_USER are placeholders. Do not run with shell tracing enabled or put tokens in a committed script. Docker stores credentials according to its configured credential helper; check that configuration on a shared host.

sections.body: Tagging gives the same local image another name; pushing uploads its referenced layers and manifest. Inspect the output digest and associate it with the source commit and tests. A tag called tested is still mutable unless the registry enforces otherwise.
sections.code:
image=registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.0
docker tag go-api:dev "$image"
docker push "$image"
docker image inspect "$image" --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'
sections.title: Publish an explicit version and record the result
sections.walkthrough: Replace owner and registry first and publish only your intended artifact. The digest from a successful push identifies the remote content. Referencing image@sha256:... in a deployment avoids relying on a mutable tag; use the full real digest, not an ellipsis.

sections.body: Buildx can build for a specified target when the builder supports it. A multi-platform image requires compatible toolchains, base images and code for each target. Setting GOOS alone does not ensure the native CPU architecture matches the Kubernetes node.
sections.code:
docker buildx ls
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 \
  -t registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.0-amd64 --push .
docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.0-amd64
sections.title: Match the image platform to the target nodes
sections.walkthrough: This command publishes a separate amd64 tag. A compatible buildx builder may need emulation or native nodes. The earlier Dockerfile compiles inside its selected builder platform; custom cross-compilation needs explicit GOARCH/TARGETARCH handling.

reading.takeaway: Publish to an owned registry namespace, retain the pushed digest and verify the target platform. A local tag or a successful host build does not prove a cluster can pull and run that artifact.

lessons.title: Publish an image: tags, digests and target platforms

summary: Build, run, inspect and publish with Docker, Compose and Podman.
title: Around Go: containers
translationNote: Use your own development machine for these command examples. Each lesson distinguishes images, instances, networking and stored data.

lessons.explanation: kubectl reads a kubeconfig and sends requests to its selected cluster as a configured identity. A namespace narrows many workload operations but does not select a cluster. These lessons assume an existing disposable development cluster with a context named dev-cluster; substitute your actual development context.
lessons.objective: Inspect the target cluster and explicitly scope commands before making changes.

sections.body: config get-contexts lists saved contexts, and current-context prints the default. A context bundles cluster, identity and an optional namespace. These commands inspect local configuration; they do not establish whether the remote API is reachable.
sections.code:
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context
kubectl --context dev-cluster cluster-info
sections.title: Identify the context before querying workloads
sections.walkthrough: Replace dev-cluster with the development context you inspected. Avoid config view --raw in shared output because it can reveal credentials. Supplying --context on later commands avoids silently targeting a different default cluster.

sections.body: get namespaces shows available namespaces when your identity is allowed to list them. api-resources tells you the kinds the server exposes. auth can-i checks authorization for one requested action; it is not a proof that the action will otherwise succeed.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster get namespaces
kubectl --context dev-cluster api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl --context dev-cluster auth can-i create deployments -n go-lab
sections.title: Find namespaces and discover resource types
sections.walkthrough: A no response from can-i means your identity lacks that permission. An absent go-lab namespace must be created deliberately by an authorized user before the later exercises. Do not switch to a more privileged production credential as an automatic workaround.

sections.body: Create go-lab only on the inspected development cluster if it does not exist. -n selects the namespace for the request. Pod queries can be watched with -w; Ctrl-C stops watching without deleting any workload.
sections.code:
# One-time setup if go-lab does not exist:
kubectl --context dev-cluster create namespace go-lab
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -o wide
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -w
sections.title: Scope a development namespace explicitly
sections.walkthrough: An empty namespace correctly reports no resources. AlreadyExists from create means the setup already happened; inspect before reusing a namespace someone else owns. Namespace deletion later would delete its namespaced resources, so it is not a casual cleanup command.

reading.takeaway: Know the context, identity and namespace before working on a cluster. Keep the development context and namespace explicit in commands; a namespace flag alone cannot protect against targeting the wrong cluster.

lessons.title: kubectl first steps: context, namespace and permissions

lessons.explanation: Kubernetes operates containerized workloads. It does not write your Go code or remove distributed-system failures. A Deployment describes the desired replicated workload; a Service gives selected Pods a stable network abstraction while individual Pods are replaced.
lessons.objective: Read Deployment, Pod labels, resource budgets and a Service without confusing them with an application build.

sections.body: This abbreviated manifest connects a Service to Pods carrying app: go-api. The image reference is a placeholder for an image you have built, tested and published to an accessible registry. Read it as configuration, not something the iOS app can apply.
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: go-api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: go-api}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: go-api}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: your-registry/go-api:tested
          ports: [{containerPort: 8080}]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}
            limits: {cpu: "1", memory: "512Mi"}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: go-api
spec:
  selector: {app: go-api}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8080}]
sections.title: Follow selectors and labels
sections.walkthrough: The numbers illustrate syntax, not capacity recommendations. This Service is internal by default; public ingress, TLS and authentication need their own design. The Deployment example still needs suitable probe and shutdown policies.

sections.body: Requests influence scheduling; CPU and memory limits have different runtime effects. Use the Pod specification and Deployment state to inspect the declared budget, then compare with metrics if the cluster exposes them. The sample numbers are illustrative rather than recommendations.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api -o wide
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'
sections.title: Observe replicas, requests and limits
sections.walkthrough: Run after the context/setup and apply lessons. Two replicas each allowing fifty downstream calls can present a hundred simultaneous calls. Resource declarations do not measure actual usage; memory exhaustion can terminate a container while CPU limits can throttle it.

sections.body: Rolling replacement and service discovery help teams operating many workloads, but cluster maintenance and debugging cost time. A VM, a managed service or a single container host can be simpler for a small application. Learn the reconciliation model before copying a large production manifest, and inspect a plan in a non-production environment before applying it.
sections.title: Use orchestration only when it pays for itself

reading.takeaway: Match labels to selectors, give each replica a resource and downstream budget, and treat public routing as a separate concern.

lessons.title: Kubernetes reconciles a workload; a Service routes to it

lessons.explanation: A manifest declares desired state; the API accepting it is only the start of reconciliation. Save the earlier Deployment and Service example as deployment.yaml, set a real pullable image reference and use the go-lab development namespace from the context lesson.
lessons.objective: Validate a workload document and observe reconciliation rather than assuming apply means ready.

sections.body: explain documents a field from the API schema. apply --dry-run=server asks the server to validate and default the request without persisting it. It still requires API access and appropriate permission and can depend on admission configuration.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab apply \
  --dry-run=server -f deployment.yaml
sections.title: Read the schema and validate with the server
sections.walkthrough: Fix unknown fields and validation errors before the real apply. A successful dry run does not schedule Pods, pull images or test your application. Only submit trusted reviewed files, including any resource namespace declared inside them.

sections.body: diff compares the proposed object with live state; exit one means differences, not necessarily a failed comparison. apply persists the desired resource changes, so inspect the exact files and target namespace before this mutation.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab diff -f deployment.yaml
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab apply -f deployment.yaml
sections.title: Review the delta and apply the intended state
sections.walkthrough: kubectl diff uses status zero for no changes, one for differences and greater than one for errors. Do not hide all nonzero codes with || true in automation. apply may create or update several documents from this file.

sections.body: rollout status waits for a Deployment update to finish within a timeout. get reports objects and their current state; it does not prove every business request succeeds. A timeout should lead to diagnosis of the existing rollout before another deployment attempt.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deploy/go-api --timeout=120s
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deploy,rs,pods,svc -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get svc go-api
sections.title: Wait for convergence and inspect the resulting objects
sections.walkthrough: The original Service example does not give the Service object an app label, so the final explicit Service query is necessary. Inspect readiness, image pulls and events if convergence fails. A successful apply alone is not release success.

reading.takeaway: Validate a reviewed document, understand diff exit codes, apply once and observe the rollout. API acceptance and a ready, functional application are separate milestones.

lessons.title: Deploy a manifest: explain, dry-run, diff and apply

lessons.explanation: Read the workload state before changing it. A Deployment, a Pod and a container can each have a different status, so diagnose the layer that is failing. These commands refer to the earlier go-api Deployment in the explicit go-lab development namespace.
lessons.objective: Find the concrete reason behind Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or an unready container.

sections.body: get -o wide includes node and Pod addresses. describe exposes scheduling decisions, container state and recent events. Copy the exact Pod name from get rather than inventing an identifier; the placeholder below must be replaced.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api -o wide
pod_name=REPLACE_WITH_ACTUAL_POD
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab describe pod "$pod_name"
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
sections.title: Find the Pod and read its events
sections.walkthrough: Pending often needs scheduling/volume evidence; ImagePullBackOff needs the image or registry failure. CrashLoopBackOff describes retry backoff after container failure, not a root cause. Check the reported reason and exit code first.

sections.body: logs reads application stdout/stderr. -c selects the container name api from the earlier manifest. --previous requests the last terminated instance when one exists, which is valuable when the current container restarted before you could follow it.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab logs "$pod_name" -c api --tail=100
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab logs "$pod_name" -c api --previous --tail=100
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab logs "$pod_name" -c api -f --since=5m
sections.title: Read the right container and the previous attempt
sections.walkthrough: No previous container is a valid reason for --previous to fail. Ctrl-C only stops following logs. Redact sensitive application data before sharing output and correlate timestamps with restarts and rollout events.

sections.body: top requires the cluster metrics API, commonly provided by Metrics Server. exec starts a command that already exists in the image; the earlier scratch Go image has no shell. For richer diagnosis, use an approved ephemeral debug image and the required cluster permissions.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab top pods -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster top nodes
# Only for an image that actually contains /bin/sh:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab exec -it "$pod_name" -c api -- /bin/sh
sections.title: Inspect resources and choose an available debug path
sections.walkthrough: A missing metrics API does not mean resource usage is zero. The exec line will fail for scratch images by design; use logs, profiles or a deliberate debug-container workflow instead of assuming every production image includes utilities.

reading.takeaway: Read exact state, events, container logs and resource evidence before restarting. Previous logs can explain a crash loop; missing metrics or a missing shell is a tooling boundary, not an application diagnosis.

lessons.title: Debug Pods: get, describe, logs, events and top

lessons.explanation: A Service object can exist while routing to no useful Pods. Diagnose its selector, selected endpoints, target port and application listener separately. This lesson uses the earlier internal Service go-api on port 80 targeting the Go container port 8080.
lessons.objective: Trace a request from a local port through a Service to a ready application endpoint.

sections.body: A Service selector matches Pod labels; EndpointSlices describe backend addresses and readiness. Deployment existence alone does not prove the Service selected its Pods. Query the named Service because the sample object does not have an app metadata label.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab describe service go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api --show-labels
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get endpointslices \
  -l kubernetes.io/service-name=go-api -o wide
sections.title: Check selector and ready endpoints
sections.walkthrough: Empty endpoints suggest a selector mismatch, missing Pods or readiness problems. Compare targetPort 8080 with the actual Go listener. A listener bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the Pod cannot normally serve traffic arriving at its Pod interface.

sections.body: port-forward supplies a temporary local development path; it is not a public ingress or load test. Bind it to loopback and keep the process running while you use a second terminal to call the local address.
sections.code:
# Terminal 1; stop with Ctrl-C:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab port-forward \
  --address 127.0.0.1 service/go-api 8080:80
# Terminal 2:
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.title: Forward one local port and make a bounded request
sections.walkthrough: The local 8080 forwards to Service port 80, which resolves to a Pod target. If another local process owns 8080, choose a different local port. The session can end when its selected Pod disappears; it does not create durable routing.

sections.body: An in-cluster client in go-lab can normally resolve go-api; a client in another namespace can use go-api.go-lab.svc.cluster.local on a cluster using that DNS suffix. Network policy and DNS configuration still apply. A port-forward does not prove the ordinary in-cluster network route works.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get service go-api -o yaml
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get networkpolicy
sections.title: Distinguish application access from a diagnostic tunnel
sections.walkthrough: Check Service type, ports and selectors in the first output. No policies in this namespace is not a complete security audit: cluster networking and other policy mechanisms can also affect traffic. Ingress, public TLS and authentication need their own configuration.

reading.takeaway: Trace labels, endpoint readiness, Service ports and the listener as separate links. Port-forward is a useful temporary tunnel, but it cannot validate all normal service-network and public-ingress behavior.

lessons.title: Service routing: selectors, endpoints and port-forward

lessons.explanation: Separate application configuration from the image artifact. ConfigMaps hold ordinary configuration; Secrets are intended for sensitive values but are not made confidential merely by base64 encoding. These development examples assume a namespace you own and the permissions to manage its configuration.
lessons.objective: Create a non-secret setting, mount a Secret reference and understand why environment changes need replacement.

sections.body: create with --dry-run=client -o yaml generates an object locally. Piping that object to apply creates or updates the named configuration on the explicit cluster. LOG_LEVEL is an ordinary non-secret value here, so showing its key is appropriate.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab create configmap go-api-config \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
  kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab apply -f -
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab describe configmap go-api-config
sections.title: Generate and apply a non-secret ConfigMap
sections.walkthrough: In a Bash script, enable pipefail and handle the pipeline status. The first command only generates YAML; the second performs the API mutation. Do not use a ConfigMap for a database password or access token.

sections.body: This is a fragment to merge into the api container in deployment.yaml, not a standalone manifest. It assumes an existing go-api-credentials Secret with a password key, supplied through your cluster secret-management process.
sections.code:
env:
  - name: LOG_LEVEL
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: go-api-config
        key: LOG_LEVEL
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: go-api-credentials
        key: password
sections.title: Reference existing config and secret keys from the Pod
sections.walkthrough: The application reads these values when its process starts. Restrict Secret access and configure storage protection at the cluster level. Never commit live Secret YAML or paste decoded credentials into a lesson exercise.

sections.body: Changing the ConfigMap does not rewrite environment variables in a running process. A controlled rollout restart replaces Pods so they read the updated values. ConfigMap volume updates have different propagation and application-reload behavior, and subPath mounts do not receive normal automatic updates.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout restart deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api
sections.title: Replace Pods when environment configuration changes
sections.walkthrough: Only restart after the reviewed configuration and Pod template are ready. Observe readiness and service behavior afterwards without logging the password. This restart changes running workloads; it is not a read-only configuration check.

reading.takeaway: Use ConfigMaps for ordinary values and controlled Secret references for credentials. Environment is captured at process startup; replacing Pods and reloading mounted files are distinct update strategies.

lessons.title: Configuration: ConfigMaps, Secrets and update behavior

lessons.explanation: A process being alive does not mean it can accept useful work. Readiness controls whether a Pod receives normal Service traffic. Liveness can trigger a restart. A startup probe can allow initialization before the other probes take effect. Choose each signal according to the failure it should detect.
lessons.objective: Give each health signal one purpose and arrange a bounded stop that drains owned work.

sections.body: Merge this fragment into the api container only if the Go server implements these endpoints. Readiness gates normal Service traffic; liveness should detect a condition a restart can repair. A startup probe delays the other probes until startup succeeds.
sections.title: Give each probe one action
sections.walkthrough: The intervals are examples, not universal budgets. A shared Redis outage should not make every liveness endpoint fail and restart all replicas. Readiness should reflect the service degraded-mode contract; test the actual handler behavior.

sections.body: This native Go fragment assumes srv is already serving in another goroutine. The signal context requests shutdown; a separate context bounds draining so an already-canceled signal context does not abort it immediately.
sections.title: Drain requests within a finite deadline
sections.walkthrough: Ten seconds is illustrative and must fit the platform termination grace period. Shutdown does not automatically wait for every background worker or hijacked connection. Stop accepting work, signal owned workers, join them, and close shared clients in a deliberate order.

sections.body: Readiness changes and endpoint propagation take time; applications can still see late requests. Make handlers safe during draining, choose how to reject new work, and verify existing requests finish or fail predictably. Persist required background work before exit. Probe intervals and thresholds should fit startup and recovery behavior instead of creating a rapid restart loop.
sections.title: Test the termination path under traffic

reading.takeaway: A health check needs an action model: route traffic, wait for startup, or restart. Graceful shutdown requires explicit ownership, deadlines and a tested drain path.

lessons.title: Readiness, liveness and graceful shutdown

lessons.explanation: A Deployment rollout changes its Pod template and replaces replicas under its update policy. A timeout or unhealthy Pod requires investigation before further mutations. These examples operate only on the inspected development go-api Deployment, using a real tested image reference in place of the placeholder.
lessons.objective: Change an image deliberately, observe revisions and understand what rollback cannot restore.

sections.body: rollout history lists retained Deployment revisions. set image changes the api container image in the Pod template. Use an immutable image digest in a real release where reproducibility matters, and keep the declarative source in sync with this operational change.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout history deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab set image deployment/go-api \
  api=registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.1
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
sections.title: Inspect history and set the intended artifact
sections.walkthrough: Replace the registry, owner and version with a published tested artifact before running. set image mutates the cluster immediately. A future apply from an old manifest can overwrite the change; version-controlled deployment configuration should describe the intended final state.

sections.body: scale changes desired replicas, not the size of an individual process. Check workload state and pressure afterwards. Requests, limits, database pools and worker concurrency multiply across replicas; an autoscaler or another controller may subsequently change the count.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab scale deployment/go-api --replicas=3
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab top pods -l app=go-api
sections.title: Scale with resource and downstream budgets in mind
sections.walkthrough: Three replicas are a syntax example, not a capacity recommendation. top requires a metrics API. Confirm the cluster can schedule the workload and downstream systems can handle its multiplied demand rather than treating replica count as free capacity.

sections.body: undo uses a retained earlier Deployment revision. It can restore the Pod template, but cannot reverse a database migration, external side effect or independently changed Secret/ConfigMap. Inspect the selected history revision and its artifact before a deliberate rollback.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout history deployment/go-api
# After selecting and reviewing an appropriate previous revision:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout undo deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
sections.title: Roll back a Pod template, then verify the service
sections.walkthrough: The undo line chooses the previous retained revision; use --to-revision with an inspected real number for an explicit choice. Afterwards verify readiness, logs and the API through a fresh test request. Do not repeatedly undo merely because a status command timed out.

reading.takeaway: Record the released image, observe the rollout and budget replicas against downstream capacity. Rollback restores a retained workload template, not databases or every separate configuration object.

lessons.title: Release operations: rollout, scale and rollback
